t: What an agent is (and isn't): workflows, autonomy and the maths of multi-step loops
sum: A precise definition of an agent (the model owns the control flow), the autonomy spectrum from one call to long-running agents, the five workflow patterns that usually beat an agent, the reliability, cost and latency maths of multi-step loops (0.95^10 = 0.60), and how to decide when not to build one.
prereq: lm16

A model calls tools by emitting a structured request (a name plus JSON arguments); your code validates and runs it and returns the result as a new message; an agent repeats that in a loop until it answers or a budget runs out.
ae2
An LLM bill is input tokens times the input price plus output tokens times the output price; output costs about five times input, and every step of a loop re-sends the whole context.
ev1
An eval is a repeatable measurement: tasks, several trials per task, graders and an aggregate; pass@k is the chance at least one of k trials succeeds, pass^k the chance all k do.
why:
A finance team asks for help with supplier invoices. Every day about 2,000 PDFs arrive by email. Someone has to read each one, find the supplier, match it to a purchase order (PO), check that the amounts agree, and either approve it for payment or flag it. An engineer, excited by a demo they saw, builds an "invoice agent": a language model with tools to read PDFs, search the purchase-order database, look up suppliers and approve payments, plus a system prompt that says "process this invoice". In the demo it is magical. It reads an invoice, searches for the order, notices a missing line, looks up the supplier's history and writes a careful note.

Two weeks into production the picture is different. The average invoice takes the agent eleven model calls and forty seconds. The monthly bill is eight times the estimate. About one invoice in twelve ends badly: the agent searched for the wrong order number and gave up, or looped re-reading the PDF, or, twice, approved a payment for an invoice whose amounts did not match because it had misread a total. Nobody can say exactly how often each failure happens, because every run takes a different path. Meanwhile a colleague rewrites the same job as five fixed steps in code: extract fields with one model call into a schema, look up the purchase order by exact number, compare amounts in code, ask the model to explain mismatches, route mismatches to a person. It costs a seventh as much, finishes in six seconds, and its failures fall into three categories you can count.

The agent was not a bad idea because agents are bad. It was a bad idea because this task has a known shape, and the agent was paying, in money, time and reliability, for flexibility the task did not need. Other tasks are different: "figure out why this customer's integration broke" has no fixed shape; the next step depends on what the logs say. There, a fixed workflow cannot cope and an agent earns its cost.

This lesson is about telling those situations apart, and about the arithmetic that makes the difference concrete. It gives a precise definition of an agent, lays out the spectrum of designs between a single model call and a fully autonomous system, walks through the five workflow patterns that solve most problems people first throw an agent at, and works the maths of multi-step loops: why ten steps at 95% each succeed only 60% of the time, how detection and retries change that, how tokens and latency grow with steps, and how to compare designs by cost per successful task. It ends with a decision procedure for when not to build an agent at all. Everything later in this track, from the agent loop (ag2) to production operations (ag14), assumes you can make that call.
primer:
Who decides what happens next?

Strip away the frameworks and the hype, and one question separates an agent from everything else built with language models: who decides what happens next? In ordinary software, your code decides. It calls function A, checks the result, then calls B or C. When you add a language model to such a program, the model might classify an email or write a paragraph, but the program still decides the order of operations. Anthropic's widely used definitions draw the line exactly there. A workflow is a system "where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths". An agent is a system where LLMs "dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage, maintaining control over how they accomplish tasks".

In an agent, the model looks at the task and what it has learned so far, and picks the next action: search the database, read a file, run a test, ask the user a question, or declare that it is finished. Your code executes that action, reports the result back, and asks the model again. The order of operations, how many there are and when to stop are decided at run time by the model. That ownership of the control flow (the sequence of steps and the choice of which comes next) is the definition. Calling tools is not: a workflow can call tools at fixed points, and an agent is only as capable as the tools it is given.

An analogy: a recipe and a chef

A workflow is a recipe. Someone who knew the dish worked out the steps in advance; the cook follows them, using skill at each step (chopping, judging when the onions are soft) but not deciding the order. Recipes are reliable, quick to follow and easy to check: if the cake fails, you can find which step went wrong. An agent is a chef handed a basket of ingredients and a goal ("make dinner for six, one guest is vegetarian"). The chef tastes, adjusts, discovers the fish is off and changes plan. That flexibility is what you want when the situation cannot be predicted, and it is wasted, even risky, when it can: a chef asked to bake the same cake two thousand times a day will occasionally improvise when you wanted the recipe.

The analogy breaks in one important way. A human chef remembers everything that happened in the kitchen. The model remembers only what is in its context window: the instructions, the tool results and its own previous messages. If your code fails to report that a step failed, the model will carry on as if it succeeded. An agent's "awareness" is exactly as good as the information your loop feeds back to it, which is why so much of this track is about what goes into that loop.

The autonomy spectrum

Workflow and agent are the two ends of a range, not two boxes. Between a single model call and a long-running autonomous system there are several useful stopping points, each handing the model one more kind of decision.

At level 0, one model call does one job: extract the fields from this invoice into a schema. At level 1, code strings several calls together in a fixed order. At level 2, a model makes one choice among paths you wrote ("this is a refund request", so take the refund path). At level 3, the model may choose tools and their arguments for a small, fixed number of steps, for example "look up whatever you need, at most three calls, then answer". At level 4, the model runs an open loop: it keeps acting until it decides it is done, bounded only by budgets. At level 5, runs last minutes to hours, may spawn sub-agents, keep memory across sessions and pause for people.

The three numbers that move along the spectrum

Moving right changes three numbers, and the rest of this lesson is about them. Reliability: every model decision is a chance to be wrong, and chances multiply across steps. Cost: every step is a model call that re-reads an ever longer history. Latency: steps happen one after another, so they add up. What you buy with those costs is coverage: the ability to handle cases nobody wrote a path for. The engineering job is to sit as far left as the task allows, and to move right only where the coverage is worth it, measured, not assumed.

If you stop reading here, keep this: an agent is defined by the model owning the control flow; that ownership is a cost paid for flexibility; and the default answer to "should this be an agent?" is "show me the cases a workflow cannot handle, and the numbers".
body:
1. A working definition, and the parts of an agent

Put precisely, an agent has four parts. A model that reads the current context and produces either an action or a final answer. A set of tools, functions your code exposes with names, descriptions and argument schemas, through which the model acts. A loop, written in ordinary code (the orchestrator or harness), that calls the model, executes requested tools, appends results and repeats. And environment feedback: the results, errors and observations that come back from the world after each action, which are the only way the model learns whether it is making progress. lm16 walked through one round of that loop; ag2 takes it apart step by step.

Two further properties distinguish a real agent from a model that happens to call a tool. The number of steps is not known in advance: it depends on what the tools return. And the model decides when the task is finished, by returning a final answer instead of another tool call. Code still sets the outer limits, called budgets: a maximum number of steps, tokens, dollars or seconds, after which the loop stops regardless of what the model wants. An agent without budgets is not more autonomous; it is unbounded, which is a bug.

A useful test when someone describes a system: ask "could you draw the flowchart of every possible run before seeing the input?" If yes, it is a workflow, however many model calls it makes. If the honest answer is "it depends on what it finds", it is an agent, at least in part.

2. The workflow patterns, one by one

Before building an agent, check whether one of the five workflow patterns from Anthropic's "Building effective agents" (December 2024) fits. They cover a surprising share of real tasks, and each is easier to test because its paths are known.

Prompt chaining splits a task into fixed sequential steps, each a model call that consumes the previous output, with optional code checks ("gates") in between. Example: write an outline, check in code that it has the required sections, write the document from the outline, then translate it. Each call does one easier thing, which tends to raise accuracy at the price of some latency. Use it when a task decomposes cleanly into stages that are always the same.

Routing classifies the input and sends it to a specialised path: refund requests to one prompt with refund tools, technical questions to another with documentation retrieval, easy questions to a small cheap model and hard ones to a large one. The classification is the only model decision about control flow, and you can evaluate it directly as a classifier with a confusion matrix.

Parallelisation runs several calls at once. In sectioning, independent parts of a task run side by side, such as one call answering the user and another screening the request for policy violations, which is faster than doing both in one prompt and keeps each instruction focused. In voting, the same task runs several times and the answers are combined, for instance three independent reviews of code for vulnerabilities, flagging if any finds one. Voting trades cost for reliability when errors are at least partly independent.

Orchestrator-workers lets a central model break the task into subtasks at run time and hand each to a worker call, then combine the results. It looks like an agent, and it is the pattern closest to one, but the structure is usually just two levels (plan, then do), and you can bound the number of workers. Example: a code change where the orchestrator decides which files need edits and a worker edits each.

Evaluator-optimiser has one call produce an output and another critique it against explicit criteria, looping until the critique passes or a limit is reached. Example: literary translation, where a critic can point out nuances the first draft missed. It works when there are clear evaluation criteria and iteration measurably helps.

Agents, in the same article's words, fit "open-ended problems where it's difficult or impossible to predict the required number of steps, and where you can't hardcode a fixed path." The guidance that follows is the most quoted line of the piece in practice: start with the simplest solution, often a single well-prompted call with retrieval, and add complexity only when it measurably improves outcomes.

3. Reliability: why steps multiply

Suppose each step of a run succeeds with probability p, independently of the others, and the run succeeds only if every step does. Then the run succeeds with probability pn for n steps. This is the same arithmetic as a chain of components in series: the chain is weaker than its weakest link because every link must hold.

Work it for a 10-step task at 95% per step: 0.95 × 0.95 = 0.9025 after two steps; 0.8574 after three; 0.7738 after five; and 0.9510 = 0.5987 after ten. A component that is "95% reliable" produces a 10-step task that works three times in five. The table shows how fast this decays.

Steps np = 0.90p = 0.95p = 0.99

200.1220.3580.818

A handy derived number is the reliability half-life: the step count at which success falls to 50%. Solve pn = 0.5 to get n = ln 0.5 / ln p. At 90% that is 6.6 steps, at 95% it is 13.5, at 99% it is 69 and at 99.9% it is 693. If your typical task needs 30 decisions, per-step reliability has to be well above 97% before the agent is right more often than not.

This arithmetic has three consequences that shape everything later in the track. First, removing steps is a reliability technique, not just a speed-up: a tool that does in one call what took three (ag3) changes the exponent. Second, per-step quality matters more the longer the task, which is why long-horizon agents need the strongest models while short routers can use small ones (ag13). Third, the formula is only true for undetected, unrecovered, independent errors, and each of those words is a lever, as the next section shows.

4. Detection, recovery and correlation

Real agents do not fail silently at every error. When a tool call has a misspelt name, the orchestrator returns an error and the model fixes it next step. When code fails a test, the agent sees the failure. Let d be the probability that a failed step is detected (by a tool error, a validation check or a test), and suppose a detected failure is retried once with the same success rate p. The effective per-step success becomes:

p_eff = p + (1 − p) × d × p

Work it for p = 0.95 and d = 0.8: 0.95 + 0.05 × 0.8 × 0.95 = 0.95 + 0.038 = 0.988. Ten steps now succeed with probability 0.98810 ≈ 0.886, up from 0.599. One retry on detected errors took a 60% task to 89%. With perfect detection (d = 1), peff = 1 − (1 − p)2 = 0.9975 and ten steps give 97.5%. The lesson is that detection is worth as much as raw quality: an agent whose errors announce themselves can be much more reliable than its per-step rate suggests, which is why tools should fail loudly with specific error messages (ag3), and why verifiers such as tests are so valuable.

Two forces push the other way. Silent errors are wrong results that look right: a plausible but wrong order number, an amount misread from a PDF, a function that compiles but computes the wrong thing. They get d = 0 and pass straight through. And correlated errors break the independence assumption. If the agent misunderstands the task in step 1 ("follow up with everyone" read as "all customers ever" rather than "people on this ticket"), every later step is wrong in the same direction, and retrying with the same context reproduces the same misunderstanding. Correlation makes the real distribution bimodal: many runs that go fine, and a cluster that go wrong from the start. That is why the most effective recovery changes something, such as a clearer error, a different tool, a re-read of the instructions or a question to the user, rather than just trying again.

5. Consistency: pass@k and pass^k

A per-run success rate hides a second question: does the agent succeed on the same task every time? Two metrics from ev1 make this explicit. pass@k is the chance that at least one of k independent attempts succeeds, 1 − (1 − p)k; it is the right measure when a person or a verifier can pick the good attempt, as with code that must pass tests. pass^k is the chance that all k attempts succeed, pk; it is the right measure when the agent must work every time, as with a support agent serving thousands of customers with the same kind of problem.

At p = 0.8 the two diverge sharply: pass@4 = 1 − 0.24 = 0.998, pass^4 = 0.84 = 0.41. The same agent is "almost always able to do it" and "usually not reliable at it". τ-bench (Yao et al., June 2024), a benchmark of simulated customers talking to tool-using agents in retail and airline domains, introduced pass^k for this reason; it reported that GPT-4o succeeded on under half of the tasks and that pass^8 in the retail domain was below 25%. When you hear an agent's success rate, ask which of these it is, and on how many trials.

6. Cost: what a run actually bills

Each step of an agent is a full model call, and the input to step k is everything so far: system prompt and tool definitions, the task, and every previous model output and tool result. If the starting context is C0 tokens and each step adds Δ tokens (the model's output plus the tool result), step k (counting from 0) reads C0 + kΔ tokens, and a run of n steps reads in total:

total_input = n × C0 + Δ × n(n − 1)/2

The second term grows with the square of the number of steps. ae2 worked this for caching; here is the comparison that decides architecture. Prices are Claude Sonnet 5.5's list prices, checked on 6 October 2026: $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.

The agent. C0 = 4,000 tokens (instructions, eight tool definitions, the invoice text), Δ = 1,000 tokens per step, 300 output tokens per step, n = 10 steps. Input = 10 × 4,000 + 1,000 × 45 = 85,000 tokens, which costs 85,000 × $2 / 106 = $0.170. Output = 3,000 tokens, $0.030. Total about $0.20 per run before caching.

The workflow. Three calls (extract, explain mismatch, draft note), each about 3,000 input and 400 output tokens. Input 9,000 tokens is $0.018; output 1,200 tokens is $0.012. Total $0.03 per run.

So the agent is about seven times more expensive per run. Caching the repeated prefix (ag5, ae2) narrows the gap a lot, since most of those 85,000 input tokens are a re-read history, but it does not close it: output, the growing tail and the extra calls remain.

7. Cost per successful task, including failures

Price per run is the wrong unit, because runs that fail still bill tokens and still need someone to finish the job. The fair unit is expected cost per task: token cost plus the cost of whatever happens when the system fails, divided over all tasks. Suppose a failed or declined task goes to a person, at $4 of staff time each (about five minutes, fully loaded).

Take the invoice case and give each design realistic success rates. The agent handles every kind of invoice and succeeds on 80% of them. The workflow handles only the 60% of invoices that match a purchase order cleanly, and on those it succeeds 90% of the time; the other 40% (missing PO numbers, split shipments, credit notes) it routes straight to a person.

WorkflowAgent
Token cost per task$0.03$0.20
Share needing a person0.40 + 0.60 × 0.10 = 0.460.20
Human cost per task ($4 each)$1.84$0.80
Expected cost per task$1.87$1.00

The agent, seven times more expensive per run, is nearly half the price per task, because it covers cases the workflow must hand off. Change one assumption and the answer flips: if the workflow covered 90% of invoices, its human share would be 0.10 + 0.90 × 0.10 = 0.19 and its cost $0.03 + $0.76 = $0.79, beating the agent. The general rule: agents pay for themselves through coverage of the long tail, and only if their success rate on that tail is good. A hybrid, the workflow for the 60% clean cases and the agent only for the rest, typically beats both: 0.6 × ($0.03 + 0.1 × $4) + 0.4 × ($0.20 + 0.2 × $4) = $0.258 + $0.40 = $0.66. (That treats the agent's 80% success on all invoices as its success on the hard 40% too, which is optimistic, so measure it.)

Two more terms belong in a full model. Risk cost: the expected damage of a wrong action, probability times impact. An agent that approves a mismatched invoice once per thousand at an average loss of $2,000 adds $2 per task, more than everything above; that is why high-impact actions get approval gates (ag10) rather than being left to the model. And variance: the 95th-percentile run may take 30 steps and cost ten times the mean, so budgets cap it (ag11, ag13).

8. Latency: steps add up

Each step waits for the model's time to first token (the delay before output begins, which grows with input length), then for the output to be generated at some tokens per second, then for the tool to run. Steps are sequential: step 4 cannot start until step 3's result is known. A rough per-step budget for a mid-size model in late 2026: 0.8 s to first token on a mostly cached prompt, 300 output tokens at 80 tokens per second (3.75 s), and 0.5 s of tool time, about 5 seconds a step. Ten steps take about 50 seconds. The three-call workflow takes about 7-8 seconds, and two of its calls could run in parallel.

That difference decides product shape. Fifty seconds is fine for a background job that emails a result, tolerable for a coding assistant showing progress, and unacceptable for a chat reply where users expect an answer within a few seconds. Agents in interactive products usually stream intermediate progress ("searching orders… found 2… checking amounts") to make waiting bearable, and push slow work to the background.

9. When not to build an agent

Put the pieces together and a decision procedure falls out. Do not build an agent, or keep the agentic part small, when:

  • The path is known. If you can write down the steps for 90% or more of cases, a workflow (with a router for the variants) will be cheaper, faster and more accurate. Use an agent, if at all, for the remainder.
  • Outcomes cannot be verified. Without tests, invariants or a grader, the agent's errors are silent, detection is near zero, and the pn decay applies in full.
  • Actions are irreversible and cannot be gated. If the agent's actions move money, delete data or message customers, and a person cannot approve them, the risk cost may dominate.
  • The latency budget is a few seconds. Multi-step loops cannot meet it.
  • Volume is high and value per task is low. At 100,000 tasks a day, $0.17 of extra tokens per task is $17,000 a day; the task had better be worth it (ag13 builds this cost model fully).
  • You have no eval set. Without one you cannot tell whether the agent beats the simpler design, so you are guessing.

10. Three products, three decisions

Invoice processing. The path is known for most invoices; amounts can be checked in code; payment approval is high impact. Decision: a workflow (extract into a schema, look up the PO by exact number, compare in code, route mismatches), with an optional agentic investigator for the 40% of messy cases that drafts a recommendation for a person rather than approving anything itself.

Customer support with refunds. Conversations vary, so some flexibility pays: the customer may need an order found by description, a policy explained, a replacement arranged. Decision: a workflow skeleton (authenticate in code, load the customer's orders), then a bounded tool loop (level 3, perhaps a 6-step budget) for the conversation, with the refund tool enforcing a policy limit in code and requiring approval above it. The agent proposes; code disposes.

Fixing a failing test in a codebase. The path depends entirely on what the code and the error say, and the test suite is a cheap, automatic verifier. Actions happen in a sandbox (ag9) and are reviewed before merge. Decision: an agent (level 4), with a step and token budget, because this is exactly the open-ended, verifiable, high-value task agents suit. It is no accident that coding agents were the first agents with large commercial adoption: they combine high value per task with cheap verification.
deep:
Verification asymmetry is the real enabler

The tasks where agents work well share a property: checking a result is much cheaper than producing it. A test suite verifies a bug fix in seconds; a compiler verifies syntax instantly; a database query verifies that a record now exists. That asymmetry converts silent errors into detected ones, which (section 4) can raise a 10-step task from 60% to nearly 90% without any change to the model. Where verification is as hard as the task itself, such as judging whether a research summary is complete or whether a strategy memo is sound, errors stay silent and agents degrade along the raw pn curve. A senior designer therefore looks for, or builds, the verifier before deciding on autonomy: invariants that can be checked in code, a re-read of state after every write, reconciliation totals, or an independent grader validated against people (ev4). If no verifier can be built, the human stays in the loop as the verifier.

Time horizons and why the frontier keeps moving

METR, a non-profit research group that measures what AI models can do autonomously (Kwa et al., March 2025), proposed measuring agents by the length of task they can complete, expressed in how long a skilled human takes. Their "50% time horizon" is the human task length at which a model succeeds half the time. They reported Claude 3.7 Sonnet at around 50 minutes and found the frontier horizon doubling roughly every seven months from 2019, with signs of acceleration in 2024. The reliability arithmetic explains why such a metric moves smoothly: a longer task means more decisions, so a modest gain in per-step reliability and in error recovery stretches the horizon a lot (from 95% to 99% per step moves the half-life from 13.5 to 69 decisions). Two cautions matter in interviews. The horizon at 80% success is much shorter than at 50%, and production usually needs the former. And the tasks are software tasks with automatic scoring, the most favourable domain for agents; horizons elsewhere are shorter.

Scaffolding has a shelf life; controls do not

Agent systems contain two kinds of structure. Some compensates for current model weaknesses: forcing a written plan before every action, splitting a task across many narrow sub-agents because one context gets confused, re-asking the model to double-check routine outputs. Some encodes the deployment's requirements: budgets, permissions, approvals, audit logs, durable execution, evals. The first kind tends to become unnecessary, and sometimes harmful, as models improve; a fixed planner can stop a stronger model from adapting to what it finds. The second kind never goes away, because it exists for the business, not for the model. Building the first kind thin and removable, and the second kind as solid infrastructure, is a design stance that survives model generations. In practice it means re-running the eval with scaffolding removed whenever a significantly better model ships.

Autonomy is a dial per action, not per system

"How autonomous is your agent?" is usually the wrong question; the better one is "which decisions does it make alone, and which need a person or a rule?" A coding agent may edit files freely in a sandbox, run tests freely, but need approval to push to a shared branch and never be allowed to touch production credentials. A support agent may look up anything about the authenticated customer, issue refunds up to $50, and escalate anything above. Designing autonomy per action, by reversibility and blast radius, lets one system be fully autonomous for 95% of its decisions and tightly supervised for the 5% that matter. The cost model from the body extends naturally: each action class has its own error rate, impact and approval cost, and the dial is set where expected damage plus approval cost is smallest.

Correlated failure makes averages misleading

Because failures correlate within a run (a wrong reading of the task poisons every step after it) and across runs (the same kind of input confuses the model every time), agent outcomes are lumpier than a per-step rate suggests. The aggregate success rate can look healthy while one slice of tasks, say invoices in a particular layout or support requests about one product, fails almost always. That has two consequences. Evaluation must be broken down by slice (ev2) and measured with several trials per task to see consistency (pass^k). And remedies should target the slice: a better tool or a workflow path for that layout fixes more than a generic prompt change.

The economics of the human in the loop

Human review is often treated as a safety cost, but it is also an input to the cost model, and it scales. If an agent completes 80% of tasks and escalates 20%, reviewer capacity sets the system's throughput: at 100,000 tasks a day and five minutes per escalation, that is 1,667 staff hours a day. Improving the agent from 80% to 90% halves that, which may be worth far more than any token saving. Conversely, an approval step on every action is cheap per action but expensive in aggregate and causes approval fatigue, where reviewers click "approve" without reading. Good designs make approvals rare and meaningful, by making safe actions safe by construction (sandboxes, limits) and reserving human attention for genuinely risky ones.

Evaluating the decision, not just the agent

"AI Agents That Matter" (Kapoor et al., 2024) showed that on several agent benchmarks, simple baselines such as retrying or escalating to a stronger model matched elaborate agent designs at a fraction of the cost, and argued that agent results should always be reported on a cost-accuracy plot. The practical lesson for a team: whenever you evaluate an agent, evaluate the simplest credible alternative on the same tasks (a single call with retrieval, a workflow, a "retry three times" baseline) and plot both on cost against success. If the agent is not on the frontier of that plot, it is the wrong design, however impressive its traces look.
prod:
How the wrong choice shows up in production

Over-agentic designs show a recognisable signature. The distribution of steps per task is wide, with a long tail, even though the tasks look similar; cost per task varies tenfold between runs; failures are hard to categorise because every run took a different path; and engineers spend their time reading traces of the agent rediscovering the same procedure. When a large share of runs follow the same tool sequence, that sequence is a workflow waiting to be written: mine the traces for frequent paths (a simple count of tool-call sequences is enough) and move the common ones into code.

Under-agentic designs show the opposite signature: the workflow's "other" or "escalate" bucket keeps growing, people add more and more special-case branches, the router's confusion matrix shows many inputs that fit no class well, and the human queue fills with cases that need a few lookups rather than judgement. That is the long tail where a bounded agent can earn its cost.

The metrics that inform the decision

Track, per task type: success rate with confidence intervals and its pass^k over repeated trials; the distribution of steps (median, p95, max); cost per run and cost per successful task; the share of tasks escalated to people and the human minutes they consume; p50 and p95 latency; and the rate of high-impact actions, with how many were approved, rejected or reverted. Plotting success rate against step count is especially telling: if success falls steeply for runs above, say, 12 steps, long runs are mostly flailing, and a lower budget plus earlier escalation will save money without losing successes.

A public case: τ-bench and consistency

The τ-bench paper (Yao, Shinn, Razavi and Narasimhan, June 2024) built two simulated domains, retail and airline, each with a database, domain tools, a written policy the agent must follow and a language-model "user" with a hidden goal. Success was judged by comparing the final database state with the expected one, a verifiable outcome. Its headline finding was not only that GPT-4o, the strongest function-calling agent tested, solved under half of the tasks, but that it was inconsistent: run the same task eight times and the chance of succeeding on all eight was below 25% in retail. That is precisely the gap between pass@k and pass^k, and between a demo and a product. For anyone deciding whether to put an agent in front of customers, the question it teaches is "how often does it get the same case right every time?", which a single-run success rate cannot answer. ag12 returns to τ-bench and its successors when building agent evals.

A well-known pattern: the reasonable-but-wrong interpretation

Many agent incidents involve no attacker and no bug in the usual sense. The agent interprets an ambiguous instruction reasonably but wrongly and the system lets it act at scale: "clean up old branches" deletes branches someone still needed, "reply to everyone waiting" emails hundreds of customers with a stale template. The common root cause is a design that gave an open-ended agent broad write access to a task a workflow, or an agent that proposes a plan for approval, would have handled. The structural fixes recur: narrow default scope, a dry-run mode that lists intended actions, a cap on actions per run, approval when a run would touch more than a handful of records, and an eval case for each such incident. ag14 covers incident review in detail.

Knobs teams actually turn

The levers, roughly in the order they pay off: move frequent paths into code; give tools coarser, task-level operations so fewer steps are needed; add verifiers that turn silent errors into detected ones; set step and cost budgets from the observed distribution of successful runs; route easy tasks to a cheaper model or a workflow; and keep humans on high-impact actions. Each change is re-measured on the eval set before shipping, because almost every one trades something, and the trade is only visible in numbers.
myths: Anything that uses an LLM with tools is an agent.

Tool use alone does not make an agent. If your code decides the sequence (classify, then retrieve, then draft) and the model only fills in steps, it is a workflow, even if one step calls a tool. The defining property is who owns the control flow: in an agent the model decides what happens next and when the task is finished. The distinction matters because it changes how you test, bound and price the system.
Agents are the more advanced design, so they are the better design.

Autonomy is a cost you pay for flexibility, not a quality level. Every decision handed to the model adds a chance to be wrong, extra tokens and extra latency. For tasks whose path you can write down in advance, a workflow is cheaper, faster, easier to test and usually more accurate. Agents earn their cost only when the path genuinely depends on what is discovered along the way.
If each step is 95% reliable, the agent is about 95% reliable.

Steps multiply. Ten independent steps at 95% succeed together only 0.95^10 = 60% of the time; twenty steps, 36%. That is why demos of short tasks look impressive and long tasks disappoint. Reliability comes from fewer steps, from errors that are detected and recovered, and from checkpoints that verify progress, not from per-step quality alone.
A smarter model will make the agent reliable, so the scaffolding doesn't matter.

Better models raise per-step reliability, but the structure around them still decides how errors compound, whether they are caught, what the agent is allowed to do and what a run costs. Public benchmarks show the same model scoring very differently with different loops and tools. Scaffolding that bounds and verifies is not a workaround for weak models; it is how any probabilistic component is made safe to depend on.
If an agent is too expensive, just use a cheaper model.

A cheaper model that fails more often can cost more per successful task: failures still burn tokens, they often take more steps before giving up, and someone has to clean up after them. The right unit is cost per successful task, including the cost of failures, not price per token. Sometimes the cheapest fix is removing steps or turning part of the agent into a workflow.
Agents remove the need for humans in the process.

Most production agents put a person at specific points: approving irreversible actions, handling cases the agent escalates, reviewing samples. The question is where the human sits and how often they are needed, which is a design choice with a cost model, not a binary. Removing the human entirely is appropriate only where mistakes are cheap, reversible or caught automatically.
lab:
Goal: see the reliability and cost arithmetic of multi-step loops by simulation, and compare a workflow, an agent and a hybrid on expected cost per task. Python 3.12, standard library only.

  1. Create ag1_lab.py. Write run_chain(n, p, d, rng) that simulates n steps: each step succeeds with probability p; on failure it is detected with probability d and, if detected, retried once (success again with probability p). Return (succeeded, steps_used), counting retries as steps.
  2. For p in 0.90, 0.95, 0.99 and n in 1, 3, 5, 10, 20, 30, simulate 20,000 runs with d = 0 and print the success rate next to the exact value p**n. Then repeat with d = 0.8 and compare with (p + (1-p)*d*p)**n.
  3. Add token cost: step k reads 4000 + 1000*k input tokens and writes 300 output tokens, priced at $2 and $10 per million. Print the mean and 95th-percentile cost per run for n = 10, d = 0.8.
  4. Model three designs with a task mix of 60% "clean" and 40% "messy" tasks: a workflow (3 calls at $0.01 each; succeeds 90% on clean, routes all messy to a human), an agent (simulated with your chain; 10 steps; pick p so it succeeds about 80%), and a hybrid (workflow for clean, agent for messy). Charge $4 for every task a human must handle. Print expected cost per task for each.
  5. Finally, add correlation: with probability 0.1 a run "misreads the task" and every step fails undetected. Re-run step 2 and watch what happens to the gain from retries.

What to look for. The simulated rates should match p**n within about a percentage point, and the 0.95 row should pass 60% at 10 steps. With detection and one retry, the 10-step rate should jump to about 89%. Cost per run should have a 95th percentile well above its mean, because retries add steps and later steps are the most expensive. The design comparison should reproduce the lesson's ordering (hybrid cheapest, then agent, then workflow) and flip when you raise the workflow's coverage from 60% to 90%. With correlated misreads, retries cannot recover those runs: the success ceiling drops to 90% whatever you do per step, which is why recovery must change something rather than repeat it.
recap: An agent is a system in which a language model decides, step by step, which actions to take and when the task is done, using feedback from tools or the environment; a workflow is a system in which code decides the sequence and the model fills in steps.

Autonomy is a spectrum, from a single call through chains, routers and bounded tool loops to open-ended and long-running agents; each move along it trades predictability, cost and testability for flexibility.

Anthropic's five workflow patterns (prompt chaining, routing, parallelisation, orchestrator-workers and evaluator-optimiser) cover most tasks people first try to solve with an agent, and should be the default starting point.

Independent step reliabilities multiply: 0.95 per step gives 0.60 over 10 steps and 0.36 over 20; the number of steps at which success falls to one half is ln 0.5 / ln p, about 13.5 at 95% and 69 at 99%.

Detected errors with recovery change the arithmetic: at 95% per step, catching 80% of failures and retrying once raises the effective step rate to 98.8% and a 10-step run from 60% to about 89%; silent errors get no such help.

Input tokens grow roughly with the square of the number of steps because each step re-sends the growing history, and latency adds up serially, so a 10-step agent is typically ten times slower and several times more expensive than a 3-call workflow.

The unit that decides whether an agent is worth it is expected cost per task including failures and the human time they create, compared with the value of the task; an agent can win because it covers cases a workflow must hand to people.
Do not build an agent when the path is known, outcomes cannot be verified, actions are irreversible and unguarded, latency must be seconds, or volume is large and value per task is small.
Agents work best where checking a result is much cheaper than producing it, such as code with tests, which is why software engineering became the first large market for them.
glossary: Agent
A system in which a language model directs its own process: it chooses which tool to call next, reads the result, and decides when the task is finished, inside limits set by code.
Autonomy spectrum
The range of designs from a single model call to fully self-directed, long-running agents, ordered by how many decisions are handed to the model.
Budget
A hard limit enforced by code on a run: maximum steps, tokens, money or wall-clock time. When it is reached the run stops or escalates.
Control flow
The order in which steps happen and the decisions about which step comes next. Whoever owns it, code or model, determines whether a system is a workflow or an agent.
Cost per successful task
Total spend divided by the number of tasks completed correctly; it includes the tokens burned by failed attempts and is the fair unit for comparing designs.
Environment feedback
Information an agent receives from the world after acting: a tool result, a test outcome, an error message. Agents depend on it to know whether they are making progress.
Escalation
Handing a task, or a decision within it, to a person or another system because the agent is stuck, unsure or not permitted to proceed.
Evaluator-optimiser
A workflow pattern in which one model call produces an output and another critiques it against criteria, looping until the critique passes or a limit is reached.
Orchestrator-workers
A workflow pattern in which a model breaks a task into subtasks at run time and sends each to a worker model call, then combines the results.
Parallelisation
A workflow pattern that runs several model calls at once, either on different parts of a task (sectioning) or on the same task several times to combine answers (voting).
pass^k
The probability that all k independent trials of a task succeed; for a per-trial success rate p it is p^k. It measures consistency, which matters when a task must work every time.
Prompt chaining
A workflow pattern in which a task is split into fixed sequential steps, each a model call that consumes the previous step's output, often with code checks between steps.
Routing
A workflow pattern in which a classifier (a model or code) sends each input to one of several specialised downstream paths.
Step
One iteration of an agent loop: a model call, plus the tool call it requests and the result that comes back.
Time horizon (50%)
In METR's research, the length of task, measured by how long it takes a skilled human, that an AI system completes successfully half the time.
Trajectory
The full sequence of model outputs, tool calls and results produced during one agent run. Also called a trace or transcript.
Workflow
A system in which code defines the sequence of steps and model calls fill in parts of it; the path is fixed in advance even if individual steps use language understanding.
drill:
Decide: the expense-report agent

A product manager wants an "expense agent" for 40,000 expense reports a month. Each report has receipts (photos or PDFs), a policy to check (meal limits, required approvals, allowed categories), and an outcome: approve, reject with a reason, or send to the employee's manager. Today, three people do this; about 70% of reports are routine (all receipts readable, all within limits), 25% need one clarification or a policy judgement, and 5% are messy (missing receipts, foreign currencies, split costs). A wrong approval costs on average $60 in recovered funds and staff time; a wrong rejection costs about $8 in employee annoyance and rework. Should this be an agent? Design it, and estimate cost per report.

Answer

Shape first. The routine 70% has a writable path: extract each receipt into a schema with one model call, check the policy rules in code (limits, categories, required approvals are rules, not judgement), approve if everything passes. That is a workflow, and the policy check should not be in a model at all: code applies rules deterministically and auditably. The 25% needing judgement (is this a business meal? is this vendor a hotel?) is a routing plus single-call problem: ask the model a narrow question with the policy clause and the receipt, and have it propose an outcome. Only the messy 5% might benefit from a bounded agent that can look up exchange rates, search past reports or draft a clarification email, and even there the agent should propose, not decide.

Where the human sits. Approvals of policy-compliant routine reports can be automatic. Rejections and anything from the judgement or messy buckets go to the manager with the model's recommendation and evidence, because wrong approvals are expensive and wrong rejections annoy people. The agent never approves on its own judgement.

Cost estimate. Workflow for 70%: say 4 extraction calls (one per receipt) at about $0.005 each plus code, $0.02 per report. Judgement 25%: add one call at about $0.01, $0.03 per report, plus a manager glance (1 minute, about $1). Messy 5%: bounded agent, 8 steps, roughly $0.15 in tokens, plus 4 minutes of manager time, about $4. Expected: 0.70 × $0.02 + 0.25 × ($0.03 + $1) + 0.05 × ($0.15 + $4) = $0.014 + $0.2575 + $0.2075 ≈ $0.48 per report, about $19,000 a month, most of it human time on the hard cases. Add risk: if automatic approvals have a 0.5% error rate at $60, that is 0.70 × 0.005 × $60 = $0.21 per report; it is worth an audit sample of auto-approvals to measure and drive that down.

What to tell the product manager. An all-agent design would cost several times more in tokens, be slower, and put judgement where rules belong, while saving almost none of the human time, which sits in the hard cases either way. Build the eval first (300 historical reports with known outcomes), ship the workflow for routine reports, measure, and add the bounded agent for the messy bucket only if it beats "send it to a person" on that bucket's numbers.
qa: E
What is the difference between a workflow and an agent?

In a workflow, code decides the sequence of steps and the model fills in parts, such as classifying, extracting or drafting. In an agent, the model decides at each step what to do next, based on tool results, and decides when it is done. The practical difference is who owns the control flow, and it determines how predictable, testable and expensive the system is. Many good systems are workflows with a small agentic step inside.

Follow-up: Is a router an agent? — Not really: a router makes one model decision that picks among code paths you wrote, so the set of possible paths is still known and testable. It sits one notch up the autonomy spectrum from a fixed chain, well short of an open loop.
E
If each step of an agent succeeds 95% of the time, what is the success rate of a 10-step task?

If steps fail independently, 0.95^10, which is about 0.60, so 60%. At 20 steps it is about 36%. The general point is that reliabilities multiply, so long tasks need either very high per-step reliability, fewer steps or detection and recovery of errors.
Follow-up: How many steps until success drops to 50% at 99% per step? — ln 0.5 / ln 0.99, about 69 steps; at 95% it is about 13.5.
E
Name the five workflow patterns from Anthropic's 'Building effective agents' and give a use for each.

Prompt chaining: draft marketing copy, check it with code, then translate it. Routing: classify a support message and send refunds, technical issues and general questions to different prompts or models. Parallelisation: check a response with several guardrail prompts at once (sectioning) or run a code-vulnerability review three times and vote. Orchestrator-workers: a coding change where the model decides which files to edit and assigns each to a worker call. Evaluator-optimiser: a translation that one call writes and another critiques until it passes.
E
Why do agents cost more per task than workflows?

Three multipliers. More model calls, because the model deliberates at every step. Longer inputs, because every step re-sends the whole growing history, so input tokens grow roughly with the square of the step count. And failures and retries that consume tokens without producing a result. A 10-step agent can easily cost five to ten times a 3-call workflow on the same task.
M
When would you not build an agent?

When the path is known in advance, because a workflow does it cheaper and more reliably. When there is no way to verify outcomes, because the agent's errors will pass silently. When actions are irreversible and cannot be gated by approvals. When the latency budget is a few seconds, since steps add up serially. And when volume is huge and value per task small, so the extra cost per task cannot pay for itself. I would also refuse to start with an agent before having an eval set, because I could not tell whether it beats the simpler design.

Follow-up: The product manager says 'but competitors have agents'. What do you do? — Build the eval first, implement the workflow baseline, then try the agentic version on the same tasks and compare success, cost per successful task and latency; let the numbers decide, and keep the agentic step only where it wins.
M
Why is the 0.95^n formula too pessimistic in some ways and too optimistic in others?

Too pessimistic because real agents detect many errors (a failed tool call returns an error, a test fails) and recover: with 80% detection and one retry, 95% per step becomes 98.8% and ten steps reach about 89%. Too optimistic because failures are correlated: a misunderstanding in step one makes every later step wrong in the same direction, and retries with the same context often repeat the mistake. Silent errors, plausible but wrong values, get no recovery at all. So the formula is a baseline for intuition, not a forecast; measure success on real tasks.

Follow-up: How would you make errors detectable? — Return specific errors from tools, validate arguments and results in code, add verification steps with cheap ground truth (tests, totals that must reconcile, a re-read of the record after a write), and log state so a checker can compare intended and actual effects.
M
How do you compare the cost of an agent with a workflow fairly?

Use expected cost per task including failures, not price per call. For each design, add token cost, tool cost and the cost of what happens when it fails or declines, usually human handling time. A workflow can be ten times cheaper per run and still lose if it can only handle 60% of the tasks and the rest go to people: in the lesson's example the workflow's expected cost is $1.87 per task against the agent's $1.00 because of human handling. Compare on the same task distribution, with confidence intervals on success rates.

Follow-up: What else would you put in the comparison? — Latency per task and its tail, the variance of cost (the p95 run, not the mean), and the risk cost: expected damage from wrong actions, which may dominate everything else for high-impact tools.
M
Explain the autonomy spectrum and where you would put a support assistant that can issue refunds.

From least to most autonomous: a single call; a fixed chain; a router choosing among fixed paths; a bounded tool loop where the model picks tools for a few steps; an open agent loop that decides when it is done; and long-running or multi-agent systems. A refund assistant belongs low on the spectrum: a workflow that authenticates the user and fetches the order in code, an agentic step that handles the conversation and proposes an action with a small step budget, and a refund tool gated by policy limits and approval above a threshold. The money movement must not depend on the model's judgement alone.

Follow-up: What would push it further up the spectrum? — Many kinds of request with unpredictable investigation paths (warranty claims needing several systems), cheap verification of the result, and tolerance for longer latency.
M
Why have coding agents worked earlier and better than most other agents?

Because verification is cheap and automatic: a test suite, a type checker or a compiler tells the agent within seconds whether it made progress, which turns silent errors into detected ones and lets it recover. The environment is sandboxable, so mistakes are reversible, and the work is text, which models handle natively. The value per task is high relative to token cost. Tasks without a cheap verifier, such as research or open-ended writing, lack this feedback loop, so errors compound unseen.

Follow-up: How would you add a verifier to a non-coding agent? — Find invariants you can check in code (totals reconcile, a record exists after a write, all required fields filled), use retrieval to check claims against sources, or add a separate grader call with a rubric validated against human labels.
M
What is a step budget and how would you set it?

A hard limit enforced by the orchestrator on the number of loop iterations, usually alongside token, money and time limits. Set it from data: run the agent on the eval set, look at the distribution of steps for successful runs, and put the budget a little above the 95th or 99th percentile, because runs that go far beyond what successes need are rarely recovering, they are looping. When the budget is hit, the agent should stop cleanly, report what it did and escalate, not just die.

Follow-up: What happens to success rate as you lower the budget? — It falls slowly at first (you cut only loops) and then sharply once you start cutting runs that would have succeeded; plotting success against budget shows the knee where to set it.
H
Design the decision process you would use to choose between a workflow and an agent for a new product feature.

Start from the task distribution: collect 100-200 real examples and try to write the procedure for each. If one procedure, or a router plus a handful, covers 90% or more, build the workflow. If the paths branch on what is discovered, prototype an agent. Then compare both on the same eval with several trials per task: success rate with intervals, pass^k for consistency, cost per successful task including the human cost of failures, p95 latency, and the worst failures by severity. Check the safety envelope: what can the agent do that the workflow could not, and can it be bounded with permissions and approvals? Decide on the numbers, and often the answer is a hybrid: workflow skeleton, agentic step for the long tail.

Follow-up: How do you keep the decision current as models improve? — Re-run the comparison on each major model upgrade; better models move the break-even point, and some workflow steps can be collapsed into the agent, while some agent steps become reliable enough to drop their checks.
H
An agent has 85% task success but costs four times the budget. Walk through how you would cut cost without losing success.

First measure where tokens go per step: system prompt and tool definitions, accumulated history, large tool results, reasoning tokens. Then attack the biggest terms. Cache the stable prefix so re-sent history is billed at the cache-read rate. Trim tool results to the fields the model needs. Compact old history. Cap reasoning effort per step type. Reduce steps by giving the agent better, coarser tools or by moving known sub-paths into code. Route easy steps or easy tasks to a cheaper model, verified on the eval. Set step budgets at the right percentile so loops die early. Re-measure success with intervals after each change, because some cuts lose quality silently.

Follow-up: Which of those usually gives the biggest single win? — For long runs, prompt caching, because most input tokens are a re-sent prefix; on current Claude pricing a cache read is a tenth of the input price for most models. Reducing steps is next, because it cuts the quadratic growth.
H
Your agent succeeds 80% of the time per run. A customer needs it to work every time on the same weekly task. What does that imply?

A per-run rate of 80% says nothing about consistency on one task. If runs on that task were independent at 80%, the chance it works four weeks in a row is 0.8^4, about 41%. That is the pass^k view, which τ-bench introduced for exactly this reason: GPT-4o solved under half of retail tasks and fewer than a quarter consistently over 8 trials. For a recurring task I would measure pass^k on that task family, reduce variance (lower temperature, more deterministic tools, a workflow for the stable part), add verification so failures are detected and retried within the run, and give the customer a review step until consistency is demonstrated.

Follow-up: Why not just run it three times and take the majority? — Voting helps when errors are independent and the answer can be compared, as with a classification; it does not help when runs make different side effects, and correlated errors make all three wrong together.
H
How do improving models change agent design, and what should you avoid building because of that?

Per-step reliability and the length of tasks models can complete keep rising; METR measured the 50% time horizon of frontier models doubling roughly every seven months between 2019 and early 2025. That means elaborate scaffolding that compensates for current weaknesses (rigid plans, heavy prompt-level validation, many narrow sub-agents) may become unnecessary or even harmful, while structural controls stay valuable: permissions, approvals, budgets, durable execution, tracing and evals. So build the controls as infrastructure, keep task-specific scaffolding thin and easy to remove, and re-evaluate on each model generation.

Follow-up: Give an example of scaffolding that later hurts. — A fixed planner that forces the model to write a full step list up front can stop a stronger model from adapting when it learns something new; measured on evals, removing it can raise success.
refs: The workflow-versus-agent definitions, the five workflow patterns, when to use agents and frameworks, and the agent-computer interface appendix. The source for most of this lesson's vocabulary.
ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models (Yao et al., ICLR 2023)
The reason-act-observe loop that most agents still follow; covered in lm16 and taken further in ag2.
Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks (Kwa et al., METR, 2025)
The 50% time-horizon metric: Claude 3.7 Sonnet around 50 minutes, frontier horizons doubling about every seven months since 2019.
τ-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains (Yao et al., 2024)
Introduces pass^k; GPT-4o succeeds on under half of tasks and pass^8 is below 25% in the retail domain.
AI Agents That Matter (Kapoor et al., 2024)
Argues agent evaluations must report cost alongside accuracy; simple baselines often match complex agents at a fraction of the cost.
Per-model input, output and cache prices used in this lesson's cost examples; prices change, so keep them in configuration.

t: The agent loop: ReAct, plan-and-execute, reflection and stopping conditions
sum: The agent loop in code and on the wire: a full three-tool ReAct episode as real message JSON with token counts, how tool calls and results are paired in the history, stop reasons and the stopping conditions a loop needs, plan-and-execute versus ReAct, and when reflection helps, with ReAct's own error analysis as the case.
prereq: ag1
An agent is a system where the model owns the control flow: it picks the next action and decides when it is done, inside budgets set by code; steps multiply errors, tokens and latency.
lm16
A tool is described by a name, a description and a JSON Schema; the model emits a structured call; the application validates, executes and returns the result as a new message.
ae4
JSON Schema describes the shape of structured data; constrained decoding or strict mode can guarantee a call matches its schema, but not that its values are right.
lm1
Chat models see a single token stream in which a chat template marks roles (system, user, assistant) and special blocks such as tool calls and tool results.
why:
The first agent most engineers write is about forty lines long, and it works on the first try. A user asks a question, the model asks for a tool, the code runs it, the model answers. Then it meets real traffic. One afternoon every request starts failing with an HTTP 400 error, "tool_use ids were found without tool_result blocks immediately after", because a new code path logged a message between the model's tool call and its result. The next week a support customer is told their refund has been issued when the refund service actually timed out; the loop caught the exception and returned an empty string, so the model saw what looked like success. A research agent burns $40 overnight calling the same search with slightly different wording 300 times. A coding agent's long file edit is cut off by the output limit mid-JSON and the loop crashes trying to parse half a tool call.

None of these failures is about the model being unintelligent. Each is about the loop: the short piece of ordinary code that sits between the model and the world, decides what the model sees, executes what it asks for, and decides when to stop. ag1 established that an agent is defined by the model owning the control flow. The loop is what that ownership runs inside, and its details decide whether the agent is reliable, affordable and honest about what it did.

This lesson takes the loop apart. It starts with the shape of the loop as code and the exact representation of tool calls in the message history, using a complete three-tool episode written out as the JSON that actually travels to and from the API, with token counts per call. It then covers the stop reasons a response can carry and the stopping conditions a loop must add of its own; the ReAct pattern in detail, including what its own authors found goes wrong; the plan-and-execute alternative and when it is cheaper; and reflection, which helps only when there is something real to reflect on. The case is the ReAct paper's error analysis, which predicted the looping failure you will meet in production.
primer:
A detective's notebook

Picture a detective who cannot leave the office and has no memory between visits, but has an assistant who can go anywhere. Every time the detective is consulted, the assistant hands over the whole case notebook: the original question, every note the detective wrote, every errand the detective ordered, and every report the assistant brought back. The detective reads it all, writes a new note ("the butler's alibi depends on the train time"), and either orders one more errand ("check the 6:15 timetable") or writes the solution. The assistant runs the errand, pastes the report into the notebook, and comes back.

That is an agent loop. The detective is the model. The notebook is the message history, and because the detective has no memory, the notebook is the entire state of the investigation. The errands are tool calls; the reports are tool results, also called observations. The assistant is the loop: your code, which decides whether each errand is allowed, runs it, writes down exactly what happened, including failures, and decides when the investigation has gone on long enough.

The analogy shows two things that are easy to miss. First, the detective only knows what is in the notebook. If the assistant writes "timetable checked" when the station was closed, the detective will reason from a fiction. Honest, specific observations are the assistant's main job. Second, the notebook grows with every visit, and the detective re-reads all of it every time. Long investigations get slow and expensive for that reason alone.

Where the analogy breaks: a real detective decides how long to investigate based on judgement and a sense of cost. The model has no inherent sense of cost and only a rough sense of progress, so the assistant must impose limits from outside.

The loop as a picture

Each pass through the loop is one step. The model's response carries a stop reason, a field saying why it stopped generating: because it finished, because it wants a tool run, because it hit its output limit, or because it refused. The loop branches on that. Tool requests go through validation and execution, and their results are appended to the history. Then the loop checks its budgets and goes round again.

Three families of loop

Within this skeleton, there are three broad ways to organise the model's thinking. In ReAct (reason and act), the model decides one action at a time, seeing every result before the next decision. In plan-and-execute, the model writes a plan first and the steps are carried out with fewer model calls, replanning only if something goes wrong. In reflection patterns, the model reviews its output or its failed attempt, writes down what to do differently, and tries again. Real agents mix them. The body of this lesson shows each with numbers, and shows that the choice is mostly about how predictable the task's path is and what feedback is available.
body:
1. The loop in code

Here is a complete loop in Python-like code against Anthropic's Messages API, with the stopping conditions this lesson argues for. Read it once now; each part is explained below.

def run_agent(task, max_steps=12, max_cost_usd=0.50, deadline_s=120):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": task}]
    cost, start, seen = 0.0, time.monotonic(), Counter()
    for step in range(max_steps):
        resp = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, system=SYSTEM, tools=TOOLS,
                                      max_tokens=2048, messages=messages)
        cost += price(resp.usage)                  # input, output, cache tokens
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})
        trace(step, resp)                          # every call is logged

        if resp.stop_reason == "end_turn":
            return finish(messages)                # verify outcome in code
        if resp.stop_reason == "max_tokens":
            return retry_bigger_or_stop(messages)  # never run a half call
        if resp.stop_reason == "refusal":
            return escalate("refused", messages)

        results = []
        for block in resp.content:                 # may be several (parallel)
            if block.type != "tool_use":
                continue
            key = (block.name, json.dumps(block.input, sort_keys=True))
            seen[key] += 1
            if seen[key] >= 3:
                out, err = ("You have made this exact call 3 times. Try a different "
                            "approach, or explain what is blocking you."), True
            else:
                out, err = execute(block.name, block.input)   # never raises
            results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id,
                            "content": out, "is_error": err})
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})

        if cost > max_cost_usd or time.monotonic() - start > deadline_s:
            return stop("budget", messages)
    return stop("max_steps", messages)

Four design decisions are already visible. The history is a plain list you own, appended to and never edited in place, so it can be logged, replayed and resumed (ag11). The function execute never raises: it validates arguments against the schema, checks permissions, runs the tool, and converts any failure into a string plus an error flag, because an exception would end the run with the model none the wiser. Every exit path has a reason (end_turn, max_tokens, refusal, budget, max_steps), which becomes a metric. And repeated identical calls are caught by the loop, not left to the model to notice.

2. How a tool call travels: the message format

Providers differ in naming, but every tool-calling API encodes the same three things: the tool definitions you offer, the model's request to call one, and your result, linked to the request by an identifier.

In Anthropic's Messages API (as documented on 6 October 2026), a message's content is a list of typed content blocks. An assistant message that calls a tool contains a tool_use block with three fields: id (a unique string such as toolu_01…), name, and input, a JSON object matching the tool's input_schema. The response's stop_reason is "tool_use". Your reply is a user message whose content contains a tool_result block with the matching tool_use_id, the content (a string or a list of text, image or document blocks), and optionally "is_error": true.

Three rules from the documentation matter for loop code. The tool results must immediately follow the assistant message that requested them; nothing may come between. In that user message, the tool_result blocks must come first, with any text after them. And when the model requests several tools in one turn (parallel tool use), all their results go in that one user message. Break the first two and the API returns a 400 error; break the pairing silently, for example by attaching results to the wrong ids, and the model will reason from swapped data.

OpenAI's Responses API encodes the same idea differently: the model's output contains a function_call item with a call_id, a name and arguments, which is a JSON string you must parse rather than an object; you return a function_call_output item with the same call_id and an output string. The parse step is one more place to handle malformed output, unless strict mode (ae4) guarantees the schema. Libraries and protocols that sit above these APIs, including MCP (ag4), translate between such formats, but the loop logic is identical.

3. A full ReAct episode, on the wire

Here is a complete three-tool episode, written as the request bodies the loop sends. The task: a customer, already authenticated as C-881 by the application, writes "Order A17, the headphones arrived with the left side dead. Can I get half my money back?" Three tools are offered: lookup_order(order_id), get_refund_policy(category, reason) and issue_refund(order_id, amount, reason). The system prompt and tool definitions are about 1,230 tokens including the provider's tool-use system prompt (286 tokens on Claude Sonnet 5.5 per Anthropic's pricing page).

Call 1. The request carries the system prompt, the tools and one message:

"messages": [
  {"role": "user", "content": "Order A17, the headphones arrived with the left side dead. Can I get half my money back?"}
]

The response (about 70 output tokens):

{"role": "assistant", "stop_reason": "tool_use", "content": [
  {"type": "text", "text": "I'll look up order A17 first."},
  {"type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_01", "name": "lookup_order",
   "input": {"order_id": "A17"}}
]}

The loop checks that A17 belongs to customer C-881 (the authenticated identity comes from the application, never from the model), runs the lookup and appends two messages: the assistant message above, unchanged, and a user message with the result.

Call 2. The request now carries three messages:

"messages": [
  {"role": "user", "content": "Order A17, the headphones arrived ... half my money back?"},
  {"role": "assistant", "content": [
    {"type": "text", "text": "I'll look up order A17 first."},
    {"type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_01", "name": "lookup_order", "input": {"order_id": "A17"}}]},
  {"role": "user", "content": [
    {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "toolu_01",
     "content": "{\"order_id\":\"A17\",\"item\":\"Aria headphones\",\"category\":\"audio\",\"price\":120.00,\"currency\":\"GBP\",\"delivered\":\"2026-09-28\",\"status\":\"delivered\"}"}]}
]

The response (about 75 tokens) reasons from the observation and asks for the policy:

{"role": "assistant", "stop_reason": "tool_use", "content": [
  {"type": "text", "text": "Delivered 2026-09-28, 8 days ago, audio category. Checking the policy for items damaged on arrival."},
  {"type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_02", "name": "get_refund_policy",
   "input": {"category": "audio", "reason": "damaged_on_arrival"}}
]}

Call 3 appends that message and the result {"window_days":30,"partial_refund_max_pct":50,"photo_required":false} (about 55 tokens) as toolu_02's tool_result. The model now has everything it needs:

{"role": "assistant", "stop_reason": "tool_use", "content": [
  {"type": "text", "text": "Within the 30-day window; partial refunds up to 50% are allowed. 50% of 120.00 is 60.00."},
  {"type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_03", "name": "issue_refund",
   "input": {"order_id": "A17", "amount": 60.00, "reason": "damaged_on_arrival"}}
]}

Before executing, the loop applies business rules in code: the amount is at most 50% of the recorded price, the order belongs to the customer, the refund is under the auto-approval limit (say £75), and the call carries an idempotency key derived from the run and step so a retry cannot refund twice (ag3, ag11). It runs and returns {"refund_id":"R-5521","status":"issued","amount":60.00}.

Call 4 carries all seven earlier messages. The response has stop_reason: "end_turn" and a text block: "I've issued a refund of £60.00 (half the £120.00 price) for order A17, reference R-5521. It should reach your card in 3-5 working days." The loop then verifies in code that refund R-5521 exists for A17 with amount 60.00 before telling the customer anything is done.

The token arithmetic. With the prefix at 1,230 tokens and the user message at 40, here is what each call reads and writes:

CallInput tokensOf which new since last callOutput tokens
11,2701,27070
21,425155 (assistant 70 + result 85)75
31,555130 (75 + 55)80
