Input cost falls from $1.21 to $0.245, about 80%. Notice that writes and reads cost about the same here: in an agent, each new token is paid once at the premium and then read cheaply many times, so the saving depends on how many later steps re-read it. On Claude Opus 5.5 ($4 input, $5 write, $0.20 read) the same run's input falls from $2.42 to $0.38, about 84%, because its cache reads are a twentieth of input.

Now combine caching with compaction. Each compaction rewrites history after the stable 6,500-token prefix, so everything after it must be written to cache again, and the summary call adds its own cost (about $0.032 with caching: reading ~29,000 cached tokens, writing ~2,500, and generating 2,000 output tokens). The compacted, cached run comes to about $0.279 + 2 × $0.032 ≈ $0.34, slightly more than the $0.305 of the uncompacted cached run.

The lesson generalises. Compaction and clearing edit history, and any edit invalidates the cache from that point on. So with caching on: compact rarely and in large chunks (Anthropic's clear_at_least parameter exists for this reason), keep the edited region as late as possible, keep the stable prefix untouched, and choose compaction thresholds for quality and window limits rather than for cost. On long runs the balance shifts back: at 100 steps, an uncompacted context would reach 254,000 tokens per step, and even at the cache-read price the re-reads, plus context rot, make periodic compaction worthwhile.

8. Designing for the cache

Most cache failures in agents come from small, innocent changes to the prefix. The checklist:

  • No volatile content in the system prompt. A timestamp, request id, user's name or "today is…" line at the top changes every request. Put such facts in the latest user message, or (on the newest Claude models) as a mid-conversation system message, which Anthropic's documentation suggests to preserve the cache.
  • Deterministic tool lists. Build tool definitions in a fixed order; tools aggregated from several MCP servers must be sorted, not iterated from a set. Do not add or remove tools mid-run.
  • Fixed settings within a run. Changing tool_choice, thinking or effort settings between steps invalidates parts of the cache.
  • Append-only history. Never rewrite earlier messages casually; batch any clearing or compaction.
  • Lifetime that matches the pauses. If steps can wait longer than five minutes (slow tools, human approvals), the five-minute cache expires; a one-hour lifetime costs 2× on writes but avoids a full rewrite after every pause.
  • Measure. Log the three usage fields per step and alert when the cache-read share of input drops.
deep:
Why models condition on their own mistakes

A language model predicts continuations of its context, and its own earlier outputs are part of that context. If step 12 contains a confident but wrong claim ("the bug is in the parser"), later steps are generated in a world where that claim was made, and contradicting it requires evidence strong enough to overcome it. This is one reason long agent runs can drift: errors are not just persistent, they are self-reinforcing. Removing a failed attempt from the history, or replacing it with a single line stating that it was tried and why it failed, gives later steps a cleaner prior. It also explains why reflection without new evidence (ag2) is weak: the critic reads the same contaminated context.

Summaries compound their losses

A run that compacts several times summarises summaries. Each pass is lossy, and details that survived one pass because they seemed relevant may be dropped by the next, which sees them only as compressed text. After four or five compactions, the agent's knowledge of the early run can be a vague paraphrase. Defences: keep durable facts in structured notes that are carried forward verbatim rather than re-summarised; make the summary schema cumulative (sections are updated, not rewritten); keep identifiers in a separate, append-only list; and keep the raw transcript outside the window so a later step, or a person, can look something up.

Provider caching and the model's KV cache

Prompt caching is the provider exposing, and pricing, a mechanism inside the serving stack: the stored key and value tensors for a processed prefix, the KV cache of lm13. That is why caching depends on exact token prefixes (the tensors for a token depend on every token before it), why changing anything earlier invalidates everything later, and why a cache hit also cuts time to first token: the provider skips the prefill work for the cached part. It also explains provider limits such as minimum lengths and lifetimes, which reflect the cost of holding tensors in fast memory. Self-hosted serving stacks expose the same idea as prefix caching, with the same design rules.

Context poisoning and persistence of bad data

Once something enters the history it is re-read on every step until removed. That includes hallucinated facts the model wrote itself, wrong results from a buggy tool, and instructions injected through tool results (ag10). A single poisoned item can steer dozens of later steps. Context management is therefore also a hygiene tool: clearing old results limits how long injected text stays in view, and compaction with a schema that records facts with their sources (which tool, which step) makes it easier to notice and drop a fact that came from an untrusted place. It is not a security boundary, though; ag10's controls still apply.

Long context versus retrieval is an empirical question per task

There is a genuine trade-off between stuffing a large window and retrieving selectively. Long context avoids retrieval errors, where the agent never fetches the passage it needs; retrieval avoids context rot and cost. Which wins depends on the task: tasks needing synthesis across many parts of a corpus may do better with more in context, while needle-finding tasks do better with retrieval. The only reliable way to choose is to evaluate both on your tasks, measuring accuracy, cost and latency, rather than following a rule of thumb. Model generations also shift the balance, so the comparison should be re-run when models change.

Evaluating context strategies

Context changes are easy to get wrong silently: a compaction prompt that drops one constraint type will pass most evals and fail a specific slice. Useful evaluations replay long recorded trajectories with different strategies and compare task success, cost and specific failure signatures: repeated completed work, re-tried failed approaches, violated early constraints, wrong identifiers after compaction. Include "needle" checks: plant a constraint early and test whether it is respected at step 40 with each strategy. And evaluate at the step counts that actually occur in production, since strategies that are neutral at 10 steps can matter greatly at 100.

Thinking blocks and context

Reasoning models add a new kind of content to the history: thinking blocks. Providers differ in whether earlier turns' thinking is kept in context and billed as input; Anthropic's documentation (checked 6 October 2026) says its newest models keep prior turns' thinking by default, while some earlier models stripped it, and offers a clear_thinking context edit. Keeping thinking preserves the cache and the model's own reasoning thread; clearing it saves tokens but invalidates the cache at that point. As with tool results, the choice is a measured trade-off, and dropping thinking blocks inconsistently is a common cause of unexpected cache misses.
prod:
The case: Anthropic's context-engineering guide and Chroma's context-rot study

Two public sources from 2025 frame the practice. Anthropic's applied AI team published "Effective context engineering for AI agents" in September 2025, arguing that as agents run longer the core skill shifts from writing prompts to curating the whole context each step. It introduced the "attention budget" framing for context rot; recommended system prompts at the "right altitude" (specific enough to guide, general enough to give heuristics); favoured just-in-time retrieval through tools over pre-loading; and described three techniques for long-horizon work that this lesson uses: compaction (as in its coding agent, preserving decisions and unresolved issues while discarding redundant tool output, with tool-result clearing as the lightest form), structured note-taking (persistent notes such as a NOTES.md, with the Pokémon-playing agent keeping tallies across thousands of steps), and sub-agents that explore in their own contexts and return 1,000-2,000-token summaries.

Chroma's "Context Rot" report (Hong, Troynikov and Huber, July 2025) supplied the measurements. Across 18 models, accuracy fell as input length grew on tasks whose difficulty was held constant, including a trivial task of reproducing repeated words, where models under-generated, misplaced the unique word and produced tokens not in the input as sequences grew. Lower similarity between question and answer passage steepened the decline; distractors had non-uniform but real effects; and, surprisingly, models did better on shuffled haystacks than on logically coherent ones. On LongMemEval, focused inputs of about 300 tokens beat full histories of about 113,000 tokens across model families. Together the two sources make the case quantitatively: a bigger window is capacity, not capability.

Failure modes and their signatures

Cache miss storms. Cost per run jumps while steps stay flat; the cache-read share of input falls toward zero. Usual causes: a timestamp or id added to the system prompt, nondeterministic tool ordering, a middleware that edits history, or a change of TTL needs after a slow tool was added.

Post-compaction amnesia. Agents redo finished work, retry abandoned approaches or break constraints shortly after a compaction. Compare failure rates in the 5 steps after compaction with other steps; fix the summary schema and carry constraints in notes.

Context overflow. Responses fail with context-limit errors (Anthropic reports a model_context_window_exceeded stop reason), usually from one very large tool result or a long run without compaction. Cap result sizes and set a compaction threshold well below the limit.

Rot without overflow. No errors, but success falls with step count. Plot success against context length at the decision point; a downward slope says the window is too full of stale material.

What to monitor

Per step: input tokens split into cache read, cache write and uncached; output and thinking tokens; context size; size of each tool result. Per run: steps, compactions, clearings, peak context, cost, success. Fleet-wide: cache-read share of input (it should be high and stable for long runs), distribution of peak context, success rate by peak-context bucket, and the post-compaction failure rate. Alert on drops in cache share and on rises in peak context after releases.

Knobs

Tool result size limits; number of tool definitions loaded; clearing trigger and number of recent results kept; compaction threshold, summary schema and recent-steps-kept; whether notes are re-read every step or periodically; cache lifetime; and whether exploration goes to sub-agents. Tune them on replayed long trajectories, and re-tune when the model changes, since newer models tolerate longer contexts differently.
myths: With a million-token context window, context management is no longer needed.

A large window raises the ceiling, not the quality of what is inside it. Measurements such as Chroma's 2025 context-rot study found accuracy falling as input length grew, even on simple tasks, and every token in the window is paid for on every step. Agents fill windows with stale tool output and abandoned attempts; curating what stays is what keeps them both accurate and affordable.
Compaction always saves money.

Compaction removes tokens but invalidates the cached prefix after the point it rewrites, and the summary itself is a model call. In this lesson's 20-step example with caching on, compacting twice costs slightly more ($0.34) than never compacting ($0.31). Compaction's main benefits are staying under the window and keeping the context focused; with caching on, it is a quality decision more than a cost one.
Summarising history is safe because the model wrote the history anyway.

A summary is lossy compression applied by a model that does not know what will matter later. It routinely drops exact identifiers, constraints mentioned once, and the reasons an approach was abandoned, and the agent then repeats work or breaks a rule. Summaries need an explicit schema (goal, constraints, decisions, open items, exact ids and paths) and the raw history should be kept outside the window for recovery.
Prompt caching is automatic, so it just works.

Caching only applies to a byte-identical prefix above a minimum length. A timestamp in the system prompt, tool definitions in a different order, a changed tool_choice or an edit to earlier history all move the point where the prefix differs, and everything after it is re-written at the premium rate. Long-running agents need to be designed append-only and verified by reading the cache fields in the usage data.
It's best to put everything the agent might need into the context up front.

Pre-loading spends tokens on every step for information most runs never use and dilutes attention. Agents can fetch information just in time: keep lightweight references (file paths, ids, URLs) in context and let the agent read what it needs with tools, as coding agents do with search and file-read tools. Up-front context is right only for small, always-relevant material.
More context always gives the model more to work with.

Irrelevant or misleading context actively hurts: distractors similar to the right answer pull the model off course, and the model conditions on its own earlier mistakes if they remain in the transcript. Removing a failed attempt, or summarising it to one line about why it failed, often improves the next step.

Goal: reproduce the lesson's token-growth and caching numbers with a small simulator, then implement a structured compaction step against a scripted summariser. Python 3.12, standard library only.

  1. Create ag5_lab.py. Write simulate(steps=20, prefix=6500, delta=2500, out=300, compact_at=None, keep=2, summary=2000, cache=False, prices=...) that returns per-step context sizes, total input tokens and cost. With cache=True, each step reads the previously cached prefix at the read price and writes the rest at the write price; after a compaction, only the 6,500-token stable prefix remains cached.
  2. Use Sonnet 5.5 prices (per million: input 2.00, write 2.50, read 0.20, output 10.00). Run the four combinations of compaction (None or 30,000) and cache (off or on). Add the summary call cost for each compaction: read the current context and generate 2,000 output tokens.
  3. Print a table of step, context size and cumulative cost for each strategy, then the four totals.
  4. Extend to 100 steps and repeat. Then change the read price to 0.05 × input with input 4.00 and write 5.00 (Opus 5.5) and repeat.
  5. Write compact(history, scripted_summary) that replaces all but the last two steps with a summary dict having the sections from the lesson, and a check_summary(summary, recent_ids) that fails if any section is missing or any identifier (match [A-Z]\d+|[\w/]+\.py) seen in the replaced steps is absent from the summary.

What to look for. At 20 steps you should reproduce 605,000 and 372,500 input tokens, about $1.27, $0.97, $0.305 and $0.34. Caching should dominate, and compaction with caching should be slightly worse than caching alone. At 100 steps, compaction should win back in total cost with caching on, and the uncompacted context should reach 254,000 tokens per step, which in a real model would also bring context-rot problems. With Opus 5.5's 0.05× reads the case for compaction weakens further on cost alone. Finally, feed check_summary a scripted summary that forgets one file path and confirm it is caught: this is the cheap guard that prevents post-compaction amnesia about identifiers.
recap: Context engineering is deciding, at every step, which tokens the model sees: tools, system prompt, notes, task, history and the latest results, in an order that keeps a stable prefix for caching.

Without intervention an agent's context grows linearly per step and its total input grows quadratically; in the worked example, 20 steps adding 2,500 tokens each grow the context from 6,500 to 54,000 tokens and bill 605,000 input tokens.

Context rot is the fall in model accuracy as input grows, even on simple tasks; it is driven by attention spread over more tokens, distractors and the model conditioning on stale or wrong earlier content.

The strategies, from lightest to heaviest, are: return less from tools, clear old tool results, compact history into a structured summary, keep notes outside the window, retrieve just in time, and delegate exploration to sub-agents that return short summaries.

Compaction in the example (summarise at 30,000 tokens, keep the last two steps) cuts billed input from 605,000 to 372,500 tokens and the uncached cost from $1.27 to about $0.97 including the summary calls.

Prompt caching charges new content once at the write price and re-reads at a tenth of input on most Claude models; on Claude Sonnet 5.5 prices checked 6 October 2026, the 20-step run's input cost falls from $1.21 to $0.245, about 80% less.

With caching on, compaction can cost slightly more than doing nothing, because it invalidates the cache after the rewrite point and needs a summary call; compact rarely, in large chunks, and for quality or window limits.

Caching breaks when anything before the cache point changes: timestamps or user data in the system prompt, reordered or edited tools, changed tool_choice or thinking settings, or edits to earlier messages; design the history append-only and check cache_read_input_tokens.
Retrieval inside the loop keeps references in context and fetches content on demand, trading an extra step for a smaller, more relevant window.
glossary: Attention budget
Anthropic's term for the idea that a model's ability to attend to relevant information is finite, so every added token slightly dilutes attention to the rest.
Cache breakpoint
A marker (cache_control) telling the provider where a cacheable prefix ends; Anthropic allows up to four per request.
Cache read
Reusing a previously stored prompt prefix; billed at a fraction of the input price (0.1× on most Claude models).
Cache write
Storing a new prompt prefix for reuse; billed at a premium (1.25× input for a five-minute lifetime, 2× for one hour on Claude).
Compaction
Replacing older conversation history with a model-written summary so the context shrinks while the key facts survive.
Context engineering
Curating the full set of tokens a model sees at each step of an agent, beyond writing the prompt itself.
Context rot
The degradation of model accuracy as the amount of input grows, observed even on simple retrieval and copying tasks.
Context window
The maximum number of tokens a model can take as input (plus output) in one call.
Distractor
Content in the context that resembles the information the model needs but is wrong or irrelevant, and pulls answers toward it.
Just-in-time retrieval
Keeping lightweight references in context and fetching the actual content with a tool only when the agent needs it.
Lookback window
How far back from a cache breakpoint the provider searches for a matching cached prefix; 20 blocks on Anthropic's API.
Prefix
The beginning portion of a request that is identical to an earlier request and can therefore be served from cache.
Structured note-taking
An agent writing important facts, decisions and progress to a file or store outside the context window and reading them back when needed.
Sub-agent
A separate model run with its own fresh context, given a focused task by a parent agent and returning a short summary.
Time to live (TTL)
How long a cache entry stays valid without being used; Claude offers five minutes (refreshed on each hit) or one hour.
Tool-result clearing
Replacing old tool results in the history with short placeholders once they are no longer needed, keeping recent ones intact.
drill:
Diagnose: the research agent that got worse and pricier

A research agent answers analysts' questions by searching internal reports and the web. Runs average 35 steps. After a release that (a) added a line "Current time: {now}" to the top of the system prompt, (b) raised the search tool's results from 5 to 20 per query, and (c) switched from a five-minute to no explicit cache setting with automatic caching, the cost per run rose from about $0.90 to $3.10 and analysts report that answers more often cite an outdated figure that was corrected later in the same run. Explain what happened and what you would change.

Answer

Cost. Change (a) is the big one: a timestamp at the top of the system prompt makes every request's prefix differ from the previous one at the system level, so on every step the whole context (tools are before the system prompt and may still hit, but the system prompt and all messages miss) is written to cache at 1.25× instead of read at 0.1×. Over 35 steps with a growing context, that turns a mostly-cached run into a mostly-written one, roughly a threefold cost increase on input. Change (b) adds to it: four times as many search results per call, re-read on every later step, increases per-step growth and therefore the quadratic total. Change (c) is not itself the problem; automatic caching works if the prefix is stable. Confirm by reading the usage fields: cache_read_input_tokens should have collapsed and cache_creation_input_tokens risen.

Quality. More results per search means more distractors and more stale figures in the window. When a figure is corrected at step 20, the earlier version from step 6 is still there, often several times, and the model sometimes cites it, which is classic context rot: the right fact is present but competes with similar wrong ones.

Fixes. Move the current time out of the system prompt into the user message (or a late system message on models that support it), and add a test asserting byte-identical prefixes between consecutive steps. Return 5 results by default with a concise format and let the agent ask for more. Clear search results after they have been processed, keeping only those the agent marked as sources. Have the agent maintain a structured "facts and sources" note, where a corrected figure replaces the old one, and re-read it before writing the answer. Re-run the eval on replayed runs and compare cost, cache share and the rate of outdated citations before and after.
qa: E
What is context engineering and how does it differ from prompt engineering?

Prompt engineering is writing good instructions. Context engineering is deciding everything the model sees at each step of a multi-step run: which tools and instructions, which notes or memories, which parts of the history, which retrieved documents and tool results, in what order and at what size. In agents the context changes every step and accumulates noise, so curating it is a continuous engineering problem, not a one-off piece of writing.
E
Why does an agent's cost grow faster than its number of steps?

Each step re-sends the whole context, which grows by the model's output and the tool result. If the context grows by a fixed amount per step, the total input billed is the sum of an arithmetic series, which grows with the square of the step count. In the lesson's example, 10 steps bill 177,500 input tokens and 20 steps bill 605,000: twice the steps, 3.4 times the input.
E
What is context rot?

The tendency of models to perform worse as the input grows, even when the task does not get harder. Chroma's 2025 study of 18 models found accuracy fell with input length on simple tasks, fell faster when the question and the relevant passage were less similar, and was hurt by distractors; on a memory benchmark, focused 300-token inputs beat full 113,000-token histories. For agents this means stale history is not free even if it fits.
E
What are the main ways to keep an agent's context under control?

Return less from tools in the first place; clear old tool results once they have been used; compact older history into a structured summary; keep durable notes outside the window and read them back; retrieve information just in time instead of pre-loading it; and hand exploratory sub-tasks to sub-agents with their own contexts that return short summaries.
M
Work through the token growth of a 20-step agent with and without compaction.

Start with a 6,500-token prefix (system, tools, task) and add 2,500 tokens per step. Without compaction the context at step k is 6,500 + 2,500(k − 1), reaching 54,000 at step 20, and the run bills 20 × 6,500 + 2,500 × 190 = 605,000 input tokens. Compacting whenever the context would exceed 30,000, to a 2,000-token summary plus the last two steps, triggers after steps 10 and 17, resets the context to 13,500 each time, and bills 372,500 input tokens, 38% fewer, plus two summary calls.

Follow-up: Does that make compaction cheaper in practice? — Without caching, yes: about $0.97 against $1.27. With caching on, no: about $0.34 against $0.31, because each compaction invalidates the cached history and adds a summary call.
M
How does prompt caching work in an agent loop, and what does it save?

Each step's request starts with exactly the previous step's request, so the provider can serve that prefix from cache and only process the new tokens. On Claude, new tokens are written once at 1.25 times the input price (five-minute lifetime) and re-read on later steps at 0.1 times. For the lesson's 20-step run on Claude Sonnet 5.5 ($2 input, $2.50 write, $0.20 read per million, checked 6 October 2026), input cost falls from $1.21 to $0.245, about 80%. Verify with cache_read_input_tokens and cache_creation_input_tokens in the usage data.

Follow-up: What if a step waits ten minutes for a human approval? — The five-minute cache expires and the next call rewrites the whole prefix; use the one-hour lifetime (2× write price) for runs with long pauses, or accept one full rewrite.
M
What breaks prompt caching in agents?

Anything that changes the bytes before the cache point. Common culprits: a timestamp, request id or user name in the system prompt; tools listed in a different order or a tool definition edited mid-run; changing tool_choice or thinking settings between steps; editing or deleting earlier messages, including by compaction or tool-result clearing; and dropping thinking blocks. Anthropic's cache order is tools, then system, then messages, and a change at one level invalidates that level and everything after. Keep the history append-only and put volatile content at the end.
M
What should a compaction summary contain?

Everything the agent needs to continue correctly and nothing else: the goal and any refinements from the user; constraints and rules stated during the run; decisions made and why, including approaches that failed and why; current state and open questions; exact identifiers, file paths, URLs and numbers the next steps will use; and what remains to do. It should drop raw tool outputs and superseded attempts. A fixed template, filled by the model and validated in code for required fields, is far more reliable than 'summarise the conversation'.

Follow-up: How do you test a compaction prompt? — Replay long traces with compaction at different points and measure task success and specific failures (repeated work, violated constraints, wrong ids) against the uncompacted runs.
M
When would you use tool-result clearing instead of summarisation?

When old tool results are bulky and no longer needed but the rest of the history is still useful: a coding agent that read twenty files, or a research agent with many search results. Clearing replaces old results with short placeholders, keeps the model's own reasoning and the recent results intact, needs no extra model call, and is easy to reason about. It is lighter than summarisation; use summarisation when the reasoning history itself has grown large.
M
Explain just-in-time retrieval for agents.

Instead of loading documents into the context in case they are needed, keep small references (paths, ids, titles) and give the agent tools to search and read. The agent fetches what it needs when it needs it, so the window holds only relevant material and the cost of an unused document is a few tokens for its reference. The trade-off is extra steps and the risk that the agent fails to look; good search tools and descriptions mitigate that. Coding agents that grep and open files on demand are the standard example.
H
Design the context strategy for an agent that runs for two hours and makes 300 tool calls.

Stable prefix: tools in fixed order, system prompt with no volatile content, cached with a one-hour lifetime because of long tool calls. A structured progress file the agent updates (goal, constraints, decisions, done, next) and that is re-read periodically. Tool results small by design, with clearing of old results in large batches so the cache is invalidated rarely. Summarisation-based compaction at a high threshold with a fixed template, keeping the last few steps verbatim and the progress file. Exploration-heavy subtasks delegated to sub-agents that return 1-2k-token summaries. Full raw history stored outside the window for recovery and audit. Monitor input tokens per step, cache hit ratio, compactions per run and failures after compaction.

Follow-up: How would you know the compaction is losing information? — Compare success and specific error types on runs with and without compaction at the same step counts, and look for post-compaction repeats of completed work or violations of earlier constraints.
H
Your agent's cost per run doubled after a release, with the same number of steps. What do you check?

Cache effectiveness first: the ratio of cache_read_input_tokens to total input per step. A drop means something before the cache point now changes each step, such as a timestamp added to the system prompt, a tool list built in nondeterministic order (for example from a set or a dict of MCP servers), a per-step change to tool_choice, or a new middleware that edits earlier messages. Then check input size by source: a tool that started returning bigger results, more tool definitions loaded, or thinking blocks now retained. Fix the cause and add a test asserting identical prefixes across steps.
Follow-up: How do you test for prefix stability? — Serialise two consecutive requests of a scripted run and assert that the first is a byte-for-byte prefix of the second up to the new content.
H
When is it better to give a sub-agent a task than to let the main agent do it?

When the subtask needs a lot of exploration whose details the main agent does not need: searching a codebase, reading many documents, trying several approaches. The sub-agent works in a fresh context, so its noise never enters the parent's window, and returns a condensed result; Anthropic describes 1,000 to 2,000-token summaries. The costs are more total tokens, an extra layer of latency, and information loss at the boundary, since the parent sees only the summary. It fits breadth-first, parallelisable exploration, and fits poorly when the subtask's details are needed for later decisions. ag8 covers the multi-agent trade-offs in depth.
H
How do context rot and the 'Lost in the Middle' effect change how you lay out an agent's context?

Keep the window small and relevant, because accuracy falls with length. Put the stable material that must be followed (instructions, tool descriptions) in the cached prefix, and the most decision-relevant material (current goal, open items, latest results) near the end, close to where the model generates. Restate the current objective and constraints in a short progress block near the end rather than relying on a system prompt thousands of tokens back. Remove or summarise failed attempts so the model does not condition on them. And measure: layout changes should be judged on the eval, not on intuition.
