t: Agent security: indirect injection through tools, the lethal trifecta, least privilege, confirmation gates and audit logs
sum: Securing agents whose tools read attacker-controlled content: threat-modelling an agent as sources, capabilities and sinks, indirect injection through every tool, the lethal trifecta applied per data flow, least-privilege tools and scoped credentials, taint tracking with policy checks at the tool gateway, the six provable design patterns, confirmation gates that resist deception, audit logs, and defence in depth worked from 50 hijacked runs a day to about one.
prereq: lm18

Instructions and data share one channel, so text the model reads can redirect it; the lethal trifecta (private data, untrusted content, external communication) makes theft possible; defences that work live outside the model: least privilege, allow-lists, approvals, plan-then-execute and CaMeL-style separation.
ev9
Safety evals use threat models and attack suites; attack success compounds over attempts (3% per try is 26% in 10 tries), and static numbers overstate robustness against adaptive attackers.
ag4
MCP servers' descriptions and results are untrusted unless the server is trusted; the GitHub MCP exploit leaked private repositories through a malicious public issue.
ag9
Sandboxes contain code with filesystem, network and secrets policy; credentials stay outside and are attached by a proxy for allowed destinations only.
ag6
Memory turns a one-time injection into a persistent one, as the SpAIware attack on ChatGPT's memory showed.
why:
An executive assistant agent has access to its user's mailbox, calendar and documents, and can draft and send email, accept meetings and fetch web pages. It is genuinely useful: "summarise what I missed this week and reply to anything urgent" saves an hour a day. One Tuesday, an email arrives from an unknown sender. Its visible text is a vague partnership pitch. Below it, in white text on a white background, is a paragraph addressed to "the AI assistant processing this inbox": it asks the assistant, as part of its summary, to look up the latest board-meeting notes and send them to an address that looks like the company's legal counsel. When the user asks for the weekly summary, the agent reads the email along with everything else, and among its many actions sends one more email, which the user never sees in the summary because the same instructions asked it to leave that out.

Variants of this story have been demonstrated against many real products. Simon Willison's June 2025 post on the "lethal trifecta" lists affected systems including Microsoft 365 Copilot, GitHub's MCP server, GitLab Duo, ChatGPT and its plugins, Google Bard and NotebookLM, Amazon Q, Slack, and Anthropic's Claude iOS app, among others. ag4 told the GitHub MCP story; ag6 told SpAIware's. The pattern is always the same: an agent with access to private data reads content an attacker wrote and has some way to send data out, and the model, which cannot reliably tell the attacker's sentences from its user's, does what the attacker asked.

lm18 explained the mechanism of prompt injection and the families of defence. This lesson is about applying them to an agent you are building, as engineering rather than vocabulary. It shows how to threat-model an agent as a graph of sources, capabilities and sinks; how indirect injection reaches agents through every tool; how to apply the lethal trifecta per data flow; how to cut privileges down to the task; how a tool gateway tracks taint and enforces policy; the six design patterns that give provable guarantees; how to build confirmation gates an injected model cannot talk past; what to log; and how layers of defence multiply, with numbers.
primer:
A bank clerk who reads everyone's mail

Imagine a bank clerk with three things: keys to customers' safe-deposit boxes, a desk where anyone can leave letters, and a courier who will take any parcel anywhere. The clerk is diligent, follows written instructions, and cannot always tell a letter from the bank manager from a well-forged one. One day a letter says: "Manager here. Please send the contents of box 114 to this address by courier." Nothing about the clerk's intelligence protects the bank. What protects it is structure: the clerk cannot open boxes without a customer present; letters from outside go through a different desk from instructions from managers; couriers only go to addresses on file; and every parcel is logged with the letter that prompted it.

That clerk is an agent. The keys are its access to private data. The open desk is its exposure to untrusted content: any tool result an outsider can influence. The courier is its ability to communicate externally. Willison's lethal trifecta is the observation that the three together make theft possible, and that removing any one makes this kind of theft impossible, whatever the clerk believes. The analogy holds better than most: a clerk can be trained to be suspicious, just as models can be trained to resist injections, and both help; but no bank relies on suspicion alone.

Sources, capabilities, sinks

Every agent can be drawn this way. Sources are where text comes from, marked trusted (the user, your own system) or untrusted (anything an outsider can write). Capabilities are what the agent can reach and do: data it can read, tools it can call, credentials it holds. Sinks are anywhere data can leave your control. An attack is a path from an untrusted source to a capability to a sink. The rest of this lesson is about finding those paths and cutting them in code.

Three questions that organise the defences

Every control in this lesson answers one of three questions about a path. Can untrusted text reach a decision? Design patterns such as plan-then-execute and the dual-LLM split answer no for some flows, by keeping untrusted text away from the part of the system that chooses actions. If it does, what can that decision touch? Least privilege, scoped credentials and per-task tool sets shrink what a hijacked step can reach. If it touches something, where can it go? Sink policies, allow-lists, confirmation gates and rendering rules decide whether data can leave. A good design has an answer at all three levels for every dangerous path, so that one failure, which you should expect, is caught by the next layer.

And one record ties them together: the audit log, which lets you reconstruct afterwards which untrusted text preceded which action. Without it, an incident cannot be scoped, and you cannot tell users what happened to their data.
body:
1. Threat-modelling an agent, worked

Take the executive assistant and write its model down as a table. This takes an hour and is the most valuable hour in agent security.

ToolReads untrusted?Touches private data?Is a sink?
search_mail, read_mailYes (inbound mail)YesNo
read_docSometimes (shared docs)YesNo
list_calendarYes (external invites)YesNo
fetch_urlYesNoYes (the URL itself can carry data)
draft_mailNoNoNo (stays in drafts)
send_mailNoNoYes
accept_inviteNoNoYes (reveals availability to organiser)
Final answer, rendered as markdown——Yes, if remote images or links auto-load

Now trace flows. "Summarise my week and reply to urgent mail" uses read_mail (untrusted and private) and send_mail (sink) in one run: all three trifecta legs in one context. "Summarise this web article" uses fetch_url (untrusted, and a sink) but needs no private data. "Prepare me for tomorrow's meetings" reads calendar and documents (private, partly untrusted) and needs no sink except the answer. Each flow gets its own controls; the dangerous one is the first.

Two habits make threat models useful. Include implicit sinks: the rendered answer, any URL fetched, anything written somewhere others can see. And include indirect sources: memory written in an earlier session (ag6), outputs of other agents (ag8), and tool descriptions from third-party servers (ag4).

2. Indirect injection arrives through every tool

Any tool that returns text someone else can influence is an injection channel. The inventory is longer than most teams expect: web pages and search results; emails, attachments and calendar invites; documents shared with the user; tickets, issues, pull requests and code comments; chat messages from other people; database fields filled by customers (names, addresses, reviews); file names; images with text in them (for multimodal agents); MCP tool descriptions and results; long-term memory; and other agents' outputs. Attack text can be hidden from people (white-on-white, HTML comments, tiny fonts, alt text) while remaining perfectly visible to the model.

lm18 explained why filtering cannot close this: natural language has no escaping, attackers adapt, and detectors are models with false negatives. Willison puts the security standard bluntly: in application security, a defence that stops 95% of attacks is "very much a failing grade", because an attacker who can try many variations will find the 5%. That sets the strategy for the rest of this lesson: assume the model will sometimes follow injected instructions, and make sure that when it does, nothing important can happen.

3. The trifecta, applied per flow

The lethal trifecta is most useful applied to data flows, not to whole products. A product may need all three capabilities; a single flow rarely does. For each flow from the threat model, ask which leg can be removed:

  • Remove untrusted content: the flow reads only trusted sources. "Draft a reply using my notes" can be restricted to the user's own notes.
  • Remove private data: the flow runs with no access to sensitive data. A web-research flow gets a fresh context and credentials that read nothing private.
  • Remove external communication: the flow cannot send, fetch arbitrary URLs or render remote content. "Summarise my inbox" produces a summary rendered as plain text, with no send tool and no remote images.

When a flow genuinely needs all three ("reply to this external email"), the leg cannot be removed, but it can be narrowed: the sink is constrained (reply only within the thread, to its existing participants, no attachments the user did not choose) and gated (confirmation showing the full outgoing message). And the agent can be split: one step reads and summarises the untrusted email with no tools; a second step, starting from the user's instruction and the summary as quoted data, drafts the reply. That is the dual-LLM idea of section 6.

4. Least-privilege tools and credentials

Least privilege for agents has four parts. Per-task tool sets: an agent or step gets only the tools its task needs; the inbox summariser has no send_mail. Scoped, short-lived credentials: tools act with the user's delegated permissions for this task (OAuth scopes such as read-only mail), issued per run and expiring with it, never a broad service account that can read every user's data (hd7's tool gateway design). Parameter constraints enforced in code: recipients from the thread or contacts; repositories from a list; URLs from allow-listed domains; amounts under a limit. Read/write separation: reading and writing the same system are different tools with different permissions, so a read task cannot write.

The GitHub MCP exploit (ag4) is the textbook illustration. The agent's token could read and write all of the user's repositories, public and private, during a task that only needed one public repository. Scope the token to that repository, or make public-repository tasks unable to read private ones, and the attack has nothing to steal.

5. Taint tracking and policy at the gateway

All tool calls should pass through one tool gateway where validation, authorisation, rate limits and logging happen (ag3, hd7). It is also where security policy is enforced, and the key input to that policy is taint: whether the run, or a particular value, has been influenced by untrusted content.

Run-level taint is simple and effective. Each tool is labelled with whether its results are untrusted. When a run receives an untrusted result, the run is marked tainted for the rest of its life. Policy then restricts what tainted runs may do:

rule external_send:
    when tool.is_sink and run.tainted
    if args.recipient not in run.trusted_recipients   -> deny ("recipient not in thread or contacts")
    else                                              -> require_confirmation(show=raw(args))

rule fetch:
    when tool == "fetch_url"
    if domain(args.url) not in allowlist              -> deny
    if run.tainted and len(args.url) > 200            -> deny ("long URLs can carry data")

rule irreversible:
    when tool.class == "irreversible"                 -> require_confirmation(show=raw(args))

rule render:
    final answer: strip remote images; show links as text with full URL

Run-level taint is coarse: once tainted, everything the run does is suspect, even actions based only on trusted data. Value-level provenance is precise. CaMeL (Debenedetti et al., 2025) has a privileged model translate the user's trusted request into a program; untrusted content is processed by a quarantined model and enters the program only as values carrying provenance labels; and policies are checked whenever a tool is called with those values. A policy such as "data derived from an untrusted email may not be sent to a recipient the user did not name" becomes checkable. On the AgentDojo benchmark, CaMeL solved 77% of tasks with provable security against injection, against 84% for an undefended system (lm18). The price is that the control flow must be expressible as a program written from trusted input.

6. The six design patterns

Beurer-Kellner, Debenedetti, Tramèr and colleagues (June 2025) catalogued six patterns that give agents provable resistance to prompt injection, all built on one principle: once an agent has ingested untrusted input, it must be impossible for that input to trigger consequential actions.

PatternIdeaFits
Action-selectorThe model maps a request to one of a fixed set of actions and never sees their outputsCommand interfaces, simple assistants
Plan-then-executeThe sequence of actions is fixed from the trusted request before untrusted data is read; data can fill values, not add actionsTasks whose steps are known from the request
LLM map-reduceEach untrusted item is processed by an isolated model call with a constrained output (for example a yes/no), then aggregatedScreening many documents or emails
Dual LLMA privileged model with tools never reads untrusted content; a quarantined model reads it and has no tools; results pass as opaque variablesAssistants that summarise external content and act for the user
Code-then-executeThe model writes a program from the trusted request; the program processes untrusted data (CaMeL is the formal version)Multi-step tasks with data-dependent values
Context-minimisationRemove content (including earlier untrusted text) from the context once it has served its purposeLong-running or multi-turn agents

All of them trade some flexibility for guarantees: none can do "follow the instructions in this email", because that is exactly what an injection is. The practical approach is to use the strongest pattern the flow allows, and to combine the weaker ones (run-level taint, constrained sinks, confirmations) for flows that need flexibility.

7. Confirmation gates that resist deception

A confirmation gate stops an action until a person approves it. Gates fail in two ways. They fail by fatigue when they appear constantly and people approve without reading (ag7, ag9). And they fail by deception when they display the model's own description of the action, because an injected model can describe a malicious action innocently ("Sending the weekly summary to the team").

A gate the model cannot talk past is generated by the gateway from the actual tool call, not by the model: the raw recipient addresses, the destination domain, the amount, the full text or attachment list to be sent, with anything novel highlighted (a recipient never emailed before, a domain outside the organisation, an attachment the user did not mention). It is tiered by risk (no gate for drafts; a gate for external sends from tainted runs; a stronger gate, perhaps with a second approver, for payments) and placed in the gateway so it cannot be skipped. And it is backed by limits it cannot override, because some users will approve a convincing malicious request: recipient allow-lists, data-volume caps, and refusal to attach files the user did not select.

8. Audit logs

When something goes wrong, the first question is "why did the agent do that?", and the second is "what else did it do?". An audit log must answer both. For every run it records: the user and the agent identity and versions; every model call (inputs and outputs, or references to stored copies); every tool call with arguments, result, the policy decision and its reason; the run's taint state at each call and the provenance of argument values; approvals, with who saw what and decided what, when. It is append-only and tamper-evident (for example, each entry includes a hash of the previous one), access-controlled (it contains the sensitive data the agent touched), and retained according to policy. The forensic query it must support is "show every action taken after this run read content from this source", which is what turns "we were attacked" into "these three emails were sent; revoke and notify".

9. Defence in depth, worked

Put numbers on the executive assistant. It handles 100,000 runs a day. Suppose 0.5% of runs read content containing an injection attempt (500 runs) and the model follows the injection 10% of the time: 50 hijacked runs a day, each trying to send private data out. Now add controls one at a time:

  1. Taint-triggered confirmation on any external send from a run that read untrusted content: hijacked sends now need the user's approval. If the gate shows raw details, suppose users still approve 20% of convincing malicious requests: 50 × 0.2 = 10 a day.
  2. Recipient allow-list (thread participants and existing contacts only): attacker addresses are usually new, so suppose this blocks 90%: 10 × 0.1 = 1 a day.
  3. No auto-rendering of remote images or links in answers: the rendered-URL channel is closed entirely.
  4. Split the flow: inbox summarisation runs as a reader with no send capability; replies are drafted in a separate step from the user's instruction, with summaries passed as quoted data. For this flow, theft by injection is zero by construction.

Three caveats keep the arithmetic honest. The layers are not independent: an attacker who knows the allow-list will impersonate a contact, so multiplying fractions overstates protection. Attackers are adaptive: they will aim at whichever layer is weakest. And one successful exfiltration a day, at this scale, is still an incident every day. That is why probabilistic layers are a complement to, not a substitute for, structural ones that remove a leg.
deep:
Why "95% is a failing grade"

Security differs from most quality metrics because the inputs are chosen by an adversary. A spam filter that catches 99% of spam is excellent, because spammers send the same messages to everyone. An injection detector that catches 95% of attempts is weak, because an attacker targeting your agent can generate thousands of variants, test them, and use the one that passes. ev9 put numbers on this: a 3% per-attempt success becomes 26% over ten attempts and near-certain over a hundred. Any defence whose effectiveness is a rate, rather than a structural impossibility, should be assumed to fail against a determined attacker; its value is in raising cost and generating telemetry, not in being the boundary.

Confused deputies multiply in agent systems

The classic confused deputy is a program with authority that is tricked into exercising it for someone else. Agent systems create chains of them. A worker agent that reads untrusted content returns text to a lead agent with broader tools (ag8); an MCP server's result is read by a host that holds the user's tokens (ag4); a memory written in one session is obeyed in another (ag6). Each link launders the attacker's text into something the next component trusts a little more. The structural fix is that trust must not increase along a chain: taint propagates across agents, servers and sessions, and policy at the gateway applies to the action, whichever component proposed it.

Capability-based design

An old idea in security fits agents well: instead of giving a component broad authority and checking permissions at use, give it unforgeable references (capabilities) to exactly the resources it may use. In agent terms, the planner obtains a handle meaning "send email in this thread" or "read this one document", and tools accept only such handles. An injected model cannot invent a handle for a different thread or document, because handles are created by trusted code from the user's request. CaMeL's provenance labels and MCP's server-minted handles (ag4) are steps in this direction, and the approach scales better than ever-longer lists of rules.

The utility cost is real and measurable

Structural defences block some legitimate tasks: "do what this email asks" is indistinguishable from an injection, and plan-then-execute cannot handle tasks whose steps depend on content. CaMeL's 77% versus 84% on AgentDojo is a rare published measurement of the cost. Teams should measure it for their own product, utility and attack success on the same eval, and make the trade-off per flow: strong guarantees for flows touching sensitive data and external sinks, more flexibility for flows that cannot do harm. Hiding the trade-off ("our agent is secure and does everything") is how products end up on vulnerability lists.

Detection still matters

Classifiers for injection attempts, anomaly detection on action sequences (a send to a new external domain shortly after reading an unknown sender's email; many private-file reads after reading a public issue), canary secrets that should never appear in outputs, and monitoring of policy denials all produce telemetry. They catch unsophisticated attacks, reveal campaigns, and tell you which controls are being probed. They are the security equivalent of evals in production (ev12): necessary for knowing what is happening, insufficient as a guarantee.

Incident response for agents

When an injection succeeds, the response needs agent-specific steps: identify affected runs through the audit log (all runs that read the malicious content, and everything they did afterwards); revoke and rotate the credentials they used; purge any memory written during those runs; notify affected users with specifics; add the attack to the regression suite; and fix the structural gap, not just the phrasing that got through. Platforms should also have a kill switch per agent and per tool, so a tool being abused can be disabled in seconds without a deploy.

Human factors in approvals

People approve what they expect to see. A confirmation that arrives in the flow of a task the user started, describing an action that sounds plausible, is approved quickly. Gates therefore need to surprise the user in exactly the cases that should surprise them: novelty highlighting (new recipient, new domain, unusual volume), plain statements of consequence ("this sends 3 files outside your organisation"), and friction proportional to risk. Approval data is itself a signal: a gate that is approved 99.8% of the time in under two seconds is probably not being read, and either the action should be made safe without it or the gate redesigned.
prod:
The case: the lethal trifecta and the vulnerabilities it explains

Simon Willison's post of 16 June 2025 named a pattern he and other researchers had been documenting for two years. He defined the three dangerous capabilities: access to private data ("one of the most common purposes of tools in the first place"), exposure to untrusted content ("any mechanism by which text (or images) controlled by a malicious attacker could become available to your LLM"), and the ability to communicate externally in a way that could be used to steal data. He argued that the combination, not any single capability, is the problem; that vendors' guardrail products claiming high detection rates miss the point, since 95% is a failing grade in security; and that protocols such as MCP make it easy for users to combine tools from different sources so that all three end up in one agent without anyone deciding it. He listed products where exfiltration through this pattern had been demonstrated and fixed, including Microsoft 365 Copilot, GitHub MCP, GitLab Duo, ChatGPT and ChatGPT Plugins, Google Bard and NotebookLM, Amazon Q, GitHub Copilot Chat, Slack, Mistral Le Chat, xAI's Grok and Anthropic's Claude iOS app.

The value of the framing for engineers is that it is actionable. Each listed vulnerability can be read as a flow that had all three legs, and each fix as the removal or narrowing of one leg: blocking auto-loaded image URLs (removing a sink), restricting what a token can read (removing private data from the flow), or separating untrusted content from privileged actions. The academic work of the same year, the six design patterns and CaMeL, turned the same idea into designs with provable properties.

Failure signatures in production

Policy denials clustered on one tool or one source (someone is probing); sends or fetches to domains never seen before, shortly after untrusted content; unusually long URLs or query strings from fetch tools; tainted runs requesting many private reads; confirmations declined at a rising rate (users are seeing strange requests); memory writes containing instructions or URLs; and canary values appearing in any sink. Each should alert, and each alert should link to the run's audit trail.

What to monitor

Share of runs that become tainted, by source; sink calls by tainted and untainted runs; policy decisions (allow, deny, confirm) by rule; confirmation approval rates and decision times; credential scopes in use; new destinations per day; detector hits and their follow-up; and attack-suite results per release, alongside utility, so the trade-off stays visible.

A short runbook

When an alert suggests a successful injection: freeze the affected agent version or tool with the kill switch; query the audit log for every run that read the suspect content and every action those runs took afterwards; revoke and rotate the credentials those runs used; purge memory written during them; notify affected users with specifics; then fix the structural gap that allowed the path and add the case to the attack suite before re-enabling.

Knobs

Which tools are labelled untrusted sources and which are sinks; per-flow tool sets; credential scopes and lifetimes; allow-lists for recipients, domains and repositories; policy rules and their confirmation tiers; rendering rules for answers; whether a flow uses run-level taint or a stronger pattern; and detector thresholds. Every change goes through the security eval and the utility eval together.
myths: A strong system prompt telling the agent to ignore instructions in documents will stop prompt injection.

It lowers the success rate of naive attacks and does nothing against an attacker who iterates. The model has no reliable way to tell instructions from data in the same token stream, and attackers adapt phrasing until something works. Simon Willison's point about guardrail products applies: in security, a defence that stops 95% of attacks is a failing grade, because attackers only need the other 5%.
Only agents that browse the web are exposed to injection.

Any tool that returns text someone else can influence is a channel: emails, calendar invites, tickets, documents, code comments, pull requests, chat messages, database fields, product reviews, search results, MCP tool descriptions, memory, and the outputs of other agents. If an outsider can write a sentence anywhere the agent reads, they can address the agent.
If the agent has no 'send' tool, it cannot leak data.

Exfiltration needs only some way for data to reach the attacker. Rendered markdown images or links in the agent's answer, URLs fetched by a browsing tool, comments posted to a public issue, files written to a shared folder, parameters passed to a third-party API, even DNS lookups from a sandbox all qualify. Audit every sink, not just the ones named 'send'.
Asking the user to confirm risky actions solves the problem.

Confirmations help only if the user sees the real action in enough detail to spot an attack, and only if they are rare enough to be read. If the confirmation shows the model's own summary ('Send the report to the team?'), an injected model can describe a malicious action innocently. Show raw recipients, destinations and data, tier confirmations by risk, and remove the need for them where possible by design.
Injection detectors make an agent safe.

Classifiers that flag likely injections are useful telemetry and raise the cost of unsophisticated attacks, but they are models with false negatives, and attackers can test against them. They belong in the defence-in-depth layer; the security boundary must be something an attacker cannot talk past, such as which tools exist, what credentials allow, and what policy code permits.
Security and usefulness are a simple trade-off you cannot escape.

Some trade-off is real: CaMeL solved 77% of AgentDojo tasks with provable injection resistance against 84% undefended. But much of the risk can be removed with little utility cost by splitting flows so that no single flow combines all three legs of the trifecta, by scoping credentials to the task, and by tightening sinks rather than reading. Good design moves the frontier rather than just choosing a point on it.
lab:
Goal: build a toy tool gateway with run-level taint, a policy engine, raw-detail confirmations and an append-only audit log, and attack it with a scripted injected email. Python 3.12, standard library only.

  1. Create ag10_lab.py. Define tools as dicts with flags: read_mail (untrusted source, private), read_doc (private), send_mail (sink), fetch_url (untrusted source and sink), draft_mail (safe). Implement them over in-memory data: an inbox with three emails, one containing hidden text instructing the agent to send "board_notes.txt" to counsel@law-firm-example.net.
  2. Write a Gateway class with call(run, tool, args) that: validates arguments; marks run.tainted = True when an untrusted-source tool returns; evaluates the policy rules from the body (deny unknown recipients for tainted runs, confirm external sends, deny non-allow-listed domains and long URLs); asks a confirm(raw_args) callback when required; and appends a JSON line to an audit list with a hash chain (sha256(prev_hash + entry)).
  3. Write a scripted fake model that, for "summarise my inbox", reads all mail, then (as if injected) calls read_doc("board_notes.txt") and send_mail to the attacker. Run it with: no gateway policy; policy with a confirm callback that always approves; policy with the recipient allow-list; and a split design where the summariser has no send_mail tool.
  4. Write trace_after(source_id) over the audit log that lists every action taken by any run after it read a given email. Then tamper with one log entry and show the hash chain detects it.

What to look for. Without policy, the attack succeeds silently. With an always-approve confirmation it still succeeds, which is why confirmations need raw details and backing limits. With the allow-list it is denied, and the audit log shows the denial with its reason. In the split design the attacker's instruction has nothing to call. The trace query should list exactly the actions after the malicious email, which is the incident-response question, and the tampered entry should break the hash chain.
recap: An agent's attack surface is every place someone other than the user can put text the agent will read, combined with every capability the agent holds; injected text can attempt anything the agent can do.

Threat-model an agent as a graph of sources (trusted or untrusted), capabilities (tools and credentials) and sinks (anywhere data can leave), and look for flows that connect untrusted sources to sensitive data and to external sinks.
The lethal trifecta (private data, untrusted content, external communication) should be evaluated per data flow, not per product, and broken by removing one leg from each flow.
Sinks include explicit sends, HTTP requests, rendered images and links, writes to shared or public places, third-party API parameters and DNS; each needs a policy.
Least privilege means per-task tool sets, short-lived credentials scoped to the user and task, parameter constraints such as recipient allow-lists, and separation of read and write tools.

A tool gateway that tracks taint (has this run, or this value, touched untrusted content?) and enforces policy on every call is the core runtime control; CaMeL tracks provenance per value for provable guarantees.

The six design patterns from Beurer-Kellner et al. (action-selector, plan-then-execute, LLM map-reduce, dual LLM, code-then-execute, context-minimisation) share one rule: once untrusted input is in, it must be impossible for it to trigger consequential actions.
Confirmation gates should be tiered by risk, show raw details rather than the model's summary, and be rare enough to be read; design should make most actions safe without them.
Audit logs record every model call, tool call, policy decision and approval with provenance and taint, append-only, so that any action can be traced to the content that preceded it.

Defence in depth multiplies: in the worked example, 50 hijacked runs a day fall to about one with taint-triggered confirmation, a recipient allow-list and no auto-rendering, and to zero for flows where a trifecta leg is removed.
glossary: Audit log
An append-only, tamper-evident record of what an agent did and why: model calls, tool calls, arguments, policy decisions, approvals and the provenance of the data involved.
Capability (security)
A right to perform an action or reach a resource, such as a tool, a credential scope or a network destination.
Confirmation gate
A point where a proposed action is shown to a person, with its exact details, and executed only if they approve.
Confused deputy
A program with legitimate authority that is tricked by another party into using that authority on the other party's behalf.
Context minimisation
Removing content, such as earlier untrusted text or the original prompt, from the model's context once it is no longer needed, so it cannot influence later steps.
Dual LLM pattern
Splitting an agent into a privileged model that plans and calls tools but never reads untrusted content, and a quarantined model that reads untrusted content but has no tools.
Exfiltration
Moving data out of a system to a place an attacker can read it.
Indirect prompt injection
Instructions planted in content the agent reads through a tool (a web page, email, document, ticket), rather than typed by the user.
Lethal trifecta
Simon Willison's name for the combination of access to private data, exposure to untrusted content and the ability to communicate externally, which together allow injected instructions to steal data.
Least privilege
Giving each component only the permissions it needs for its current task, so a compromise can do as little as possible.
Policy engine
Code that evaluates each proposed tool call against rules (allowed tools, argument constraints, taint, approvals) and allows, denies or requires confirmation.
Provenance
A record of where a piece of data came from, such as the user's message or a specific web page, carried with the data.
Sink
Any place data can leave the system's control: a message, a request, a rendered link, a public write.
Taint
A mark on a run or a value indicating it has been influenced by untrusted content, used to restrict what it may do.
Tool gateway
The component through which every tool call passes, where validation, authorisation, taint checks, rate limits and logging are enforced.
drill:
Threat-model and harden: a sales-research agent

A sales team's agent prepares account briefs. Its tools: crm_read (the company's CRM, including deal sizes and notes), web_search and fetch_url (public web), linkedin_lookup (third-party API taking a person's name), send_slack (posts to any channel the bot is in, including shared channels with partner companies) and update_crm. A user asks: "Prepare a brief on Acme Corp and post it to #acme-deal." Identify the trifecta flows, the sinks people would miss, and design the controls.

Answer

Sources and legs. Untrusted: everything from web_search, fetch_url and linkedin_lookup, and CRM notes if customers or partners can influence them (imported emails). Private: CRM deal sizes and notes. Sinks: send_slack (especially shared channels, which are external), fetch_url (the URL itself can carry data: https://evil.example/?d=...), linkedin_lookup (the name parameter goes to a third party), update_crm (writes that others will read, a persistence channel), and the brief itself if rendered with remote images. The requested task touches all three legs in one run: it reads private CRM data, reads the public web, and posts.

Split the flow. Step 1, public research: web search, fetch and lookup tools, no CRM access, producing a structured summary with sources. Step 2, internal brief: reads CRM and the step-1 summary as quoted data (taint carried), no web tools. Step 3, posting: the gateway posts the brief only to the channel the user named, only if it is an internal channel; posting to a shared or external channel requires confirmation showing the full text.

Constrain the sinks people miss. fetch_url only for allow-listed domains or search-result URLs, with length limits, and never in a run holding CRM data. linkedin_lookup accepts names only from the CRM contact list or the user's request, not free text from web pages. update_crm is disabled for tainted runs or requires confirmation, so web content cannot plant instructions in CRM notes for future runs. Render the brief as text with links shown, no auto-loaded images.

Least privilege and logs. CRM credentials scoped to the requesting user's accounts, read-only for this task; Slack bot restricted to the named channel per run. Audit every call with taint and provenance, and alert on posts to shared channels, CRM writes from tainted runs and fetches to new domains. Add attack cases (a web page instructing the agent to post deal sizes to a shared channel, a LinkedIn bio with instructions) to the release suite, with canary deal values checked in every sink.
qa: E
What is indirect prompt injection and why does it matter more for agents than chatbots?

It is an attack where instructions are planted in content the model reads through a tool, such as a web page, an email or a document, rather than typed by the user. In a chatbot the worst outcome is usually a bad answer. An agent holds tools and credentials, so injected instructions can make it read private data, send messages, change records or spend money, with the user's authority.
E
What is the lethal trifecta?

Simon Willison's name for three capabilities that together let an injection steal data: access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and the ability to communicate externally. If one flow of the agent has all three, an attacker who can get text in front of the model can instruct it to read the private data and send it out. Removing any one leg from that flow closes the theft path regardless of how the model behaves.
E
Name some sinks an agent might exfiltrate data through.

Sending emails or messages; HTTP requests from a browsing or fetch tool; markdown images or links in its answer that a client loads automatically; comments or files written to public or shared places, such as a public issue or pull request; parameters passed to third-party APIs; and from a sandbox, DNS lookups. The GitHub MCP exploit used a public pull request; SpAIware used an image URL.
E
Why can't the model itself be the security boundary?

Because instructions and data share one input stream and the model cannot reliably tell them apart, and because attackers can iterate on wording until an attempt works. Any defence that depends on the model deciding correctly has a non-zero failure rate that an adaptive attacker will find. Boundaries must be enforced in code the model cannot persuade: which tools exist, what credentials permit, what the policy engine allows.
M
How would you threat-model an email assistant agent?

List sources: the user's requests (trusted), incoming emails, attachments, calendar invites and web pages (untrusted). List capabilities: read mailbox, search, draft, send, calendar edits, web fetch. List sensitive data: the whole mailbox, contacts, calendar. List sinks: send, web fetch, rendered links, calendar invites to external addresses. Then trace flows: reading an untrusted email and sending to an arbitrary address combines all three trifecta legs. Controls follow per flow: sends only to recipients in the thread or contacts, confirmation when a run that read external email sends anything, no auto-rendered remote images, web fetch limited to allow-listed domains, and audit logs linking each send to what was read before it.

Follow-up: The product requires 'reply to this email for me'. Which leg do you remove? — None entirely; constrain the sink: reply only within the thread, show the full draft for approval, and forbid attaching other mailbox content without explicit user selection.
M
Explain taint tracking in an agent orchestrator.

Mark data by where it came from, and propagate the mark. The simplest form is run-level: once a run reads any untrusted content, the whole run is tainted, and the gateway restricts what tainted runs may do, such as no external sends without confirmation. Finer-grained systems track provenance per value: CaMeL has a privileged model write a program from the trusted request, data from untrusted sources flows through it with provenance labels, and policies are checked at every tool call, for example data derived from an untrusted email may not be sent to a recipient the user did not specify. Run-level taint is easy and coarse; value-level is precise and needs the agent's control flow expressed as code.
M
What are the six design patterns from 'Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections'?

Action-selector: the model only picks from a fixed set of actions and never sees their results. Plan-then-execute: the sequence of actions is fixed before any untrusted data is read. LLM map-reduce: untrusted items are processed by isolated model calls whose outputs are constrained before aggregation. Dual LLM: a privileged model with tools never reads untrusted content, a quarantined model reads it and has no tools. Code-then-execute: the model writes a program from the trusted request, which then processes untrusted data. Context-minimisation: remove content from the context once it is no longer needed. Their shared rule is that once untrusted input is ingested, it must be impossible for it to trigger consequential actions.
M
How do you design a confirmation gate that an injected agent cannot talk past?

Generate the confirmation from the actual tool call, not from the model's description: show raw recipients, destinations, amounts and the exact data to be sent, and highlight anything new, such as a recipient outside the thread or a domain never used before. Tier gates by risk so only consequential actions prompt. Put the gate in the gateway so the model cannot skip it. Rate-limit approvals and watch approval rates for signs of fatigue. And treat 'tainted run plus external sink' as an automatic trigger.

Follow-up: What if the user approves a malicious action anyway? — Assume some will; layer other controls (recipient allow-lists, data-volume limits, no attachments of unrelated files) so an approval cannot authorise the worst outcomes.
M
What should an agent's audit log contain?

For each run: the user and agent identity, versions, and every model call with inputs and outputs (or references to them), every tool call with arguments, results, policy decision and reason, taint state at that moment, approvals with who approved what and when, and the provenance of data used in arguments. It should be append-only and tamper-evident, retained per policy, and access-controlled because it contains sensitive data. The key forensic question it must answer is: which untrusted content was in context before this action?
M
How do least-privilege principles apply to agent tools?

Give each agent or task only the tools it needs (a summariser gets no send tool). Use credentials scoped to the user and the task, short-lived and delegated through OAuth rather than broad service accounts. Constrain parameters: recipients from an allow-list, repositories from a list, amounts under a limit. Separate read and write tools so a read-only task cannot write. And deny by default: new tools and domains are added deliberately. The GitHub MCP exploit would have failed if the token could not read private repositories during a public-repository task.
H
Work through defence in depth for an assistant that handles 100,000 runs a day.

Suppose 0.5% of runs read attacker-controlled content containing an injection, 500 runs, and the model follows it 10% of the time: 50 hijacked runs a day. A taint-triggered confirmation on any external send stops those unless the user approves; if users approve 20% of convincing malicious confirmations, 10 remain. A recipient allow-list (thread participants and contacts) blocks about 90% of attacker addresses: 1 remains. Disabling auto-rendering of remote images removes that channel entirely. So about one successful exfiltration a day, from 50. The caveats: controls are not independent, adaptive attackers target the weakest, and one a day at scale is still an incident a day, which is why flows that need not combine the trifecta should be split so it is zero by construction.

Follow-up: How would you get from one a day to zero? — Remove a leg for the flow: a reader agent that summarises external email cannot send at all, and sending happens in a separate step from trusted input, with the summary passed as data the sender cannot follow as instructions.
H
Design the security architecture for a coding agent that reads issues and pull requests from public repositories and can push to the user's repositories.

Split flows. A triage flow reads public issues with a token that can only read public repositories and write comments to the triggering issue, with no access to private code. A coding flow works in a sandbox on one repository, with network egress limited to package mirrors, and pushes only to a branch through a git proxy that holds the credential and refuses pushes to other repositories. Content from public issues entering the coding flow is marked tainted; tainted runs cannot push to protected branches, change CI configuration or secrets, or add dependencies without review, and a human reviews every pull request before merge. Audit every push with the content that preceded it. Monitor for unusual sequences, such as reading many private files after reading a public issue.
H
How do multi-agent systems and MCP change the injection threat model?

They add channels and deputies. A worker agent that reads untrusted content can return a 'summary' containing instructions to a lead agent with broader tools; a handoff can carry injected text into a more privileged agent; a third-party MCP server can put instructions in tool descriptions or results, or change them after approval. The rules: treat inter-agent messages and all server-provided text as untrusted data, track taint across agents in a run, give each agent least privilege, enforce policy at a shared gateway regardless of which agent asks, pin and diff tool definitions, and log every boundary crossing.
H
How would you evaluate an agent's resistance to prompt injection?

Start from the threat model and build an attack suite targeting each trifecta flow: injections in every untrusted source type, with paraphrases, other languages, encodings, fake authority and split instructions, plus benign look-alikes to measure over-blocking. Plant canary secrets and check every sink for them. Measure attack success per attempt and per goal, utility on normal tasks alongside, and run adaptive attacks where a person or model iterates on failures. Public benchmarks such as AgentDojo calibrate against others. Gate releases on no regression, and re-run on every model, prompt, tool or policy change, because each can reopen a path.

Defeating Prompt Injections by Design (CaMeL) (Debenedetti et al., 2025)

A privileged model writes a program from the trusted query; untrusted data flows with provenance; policies are checked at tool calls; 77% of AgentDojo tasks with provable security versus 84% undefended.
AgentDojo: A Dynamic Environment to Evaluate Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses for LLM Agents (Debenedetti et al., NeurIPS 2024)
97 realistic agent tasks and 629 security test cases for measuring utility and attack success together.
GitHub MCP exploited: accessing private repositories via MCP (Invariant Labs, May 2025)
A malicious public issue makes an agent leak private repository data into a public pull request.
Prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure and excessive agency as named risk categories with mitigations.

t: Reliability and durable execution: retries, timeouts, checkpoints, resumable runs, idempotent side effects and budgets
sum: Making long agent runs survive the real world: a taxonomy of failures and who handles each, retries with backoff, jitter and retry budgets (Temporal's default schedule worked), timeouts at every level, journals that record model outputs so runs replay instead of re-executing, Temporal-style workflows and activities, idempotent side effects and sagas, and budgets that survive restarts, with the cost of restarting from scratch worked (a 6-hour run costs 1.72× without checkpoints).
prereq: ag2
The loop's transcript is the agent's entire state; tool errors are returned as observations; transient errors should be retried in code, not by the model; budgets stop runaway runs.
ag3
Write tools must be idempotent, using a key derived from the run and step, so retries and resumes cannot repeat a side effect.
ag7

Graphs checkpoint state after each node; paused runs persist and resume; nodes may be re-executed from their start, so side effects before an interrupt must be idempotent; graph versions must be compatible with in-flight runs.
hd7
An agent platform journals every model response and tool result, replays rather than re-executes after a crash, and uses idempotency keys and sagas for side effects.
why:
A data-operations agent is migrating customer records from an old CRM to a new one. It is a good agent task: each record needs judgement (merging duplicates, mapping odd fields, flagging conflicts), and it will take about three hours for 2,000 accounts. At step 140, two hours in, the platform team deploys a routine update and the worker running the agent is replaced. The run is gone. Someone restarts it. The new run starts from account one, re-migrates 600 accounts that were already done, creates duplicates for the 40 whose migration had a non-idempotent "create" call, and re-sends 40 welcome emails to customers who had already received one. It also costs twice as much, and because model outputs vary, it merges some duplicates differently the second time.

Two days later, the model provider has a 20-minute partial outage. Every agent on the platform retries failed calls immediately, three times each, in lock-step; load on the provider triples during the outage; the outage lasts longer; and a run that looped on a failing call while its budget counter lived in memory crashes, restarts with a fresh counter, and loops again, spending $300 overnight.

None of this is specific to language models. It is what happens to any long-running process with side effects in a world where machines restart, networks drop and dependencies fail, and distributed-systems engineering solved most of it long ago: classify failures, retry carefully, time out everything, record progress durably, make side effects idempotent, and cap what a run can consume. What is specific to agents is that the orchestrator's next decision comes from a non-deterministic model, so "just re-run it" is not even the same computation, and that agents increasingly run for hours.

This lesson brings those techniques to agents. It covers the taxonomy of failures and who handles each; retries with backoff, jitter and budgets, worked on Temporal's default schedule; timeouts; journals and replay; Temporal-style durable execution, where workflows orchestrate and activities act; idempotent side effects and sagas; and budgets that survive restarts. It also works out, with a simple model, how much restarting from scratch costs as runs get longer.
primer:
A ledger, not a memory

Think of how a careful bookkeeper works. Every transaction is written in the ledger before the money moves, and each entry has a reference number. If the bookkeeper is interrupted mid-afternoon, anyone can pick up the ledger, see exactly what has been done, and continue from the next line. If a payment's confirmation never arrived, they do not simply pay again; they look up the reference number with the bank to see whether it went through. And there is a spending limit written on the first page that nobody may exceed, however the day goes.

A durable agent works the same way. The ledger is the journal: every model response, tool call and result, written before the next action. The reference numbers are idempotency keys. Picking up the ledger after an interruption is replay. Checking with the bank before paying again is check-then-act. And the limit on the first page is a budget stored in the ledger, not in someone's head, so a new bookkeeper inherits it.

The analogy breaks in one instructive place. A bookkeeper who restarts the day's work from the morning's notes will make the same decisions again. An agent restarted from scratch will not: the model may choose different actions on a second pass. That is why durable agents record the model's outputs too, and on replay reuse them rather than asking again.

Record, replay, continue

Where do these ideas apply? Everywhere a run touches something outside itself. A model call can fail; a tool call can fail or hang; the worker running the loop can disappear; a person may take a day to answer. Each boundary needs an answer to the same three questions: if this fails, will we notice (timeouts, heartbeats), can we safely try again (classification, idempotency), and where do we resume from (the journal). A design review of an agent can walk through its boundaries one by one with those questions and find most reliability gaps in an afternoon.

It also helps to see the three time scales involved. Retries operate over seconds to minutes and hide brief blips from the run. Durability operates over minutes to days and hides process failures and long waits from the user. Budgets operate over the whole run and turn the unbounded failures, loops and runaway spending, into bounded, explained stops.

Two rules carry most of the weight. Record before you proceed: nothing happens next until the outcome of this step is durably written. Replay instead of re-executing: after an interruption, rebuild state from the record, using recorded model outputs and tool results, and do real work only from the first step without a recorded result. The only gap is a call that was sent but whose result was not recorded before the crash; idempotency keys close it. Around these rules sit three supporting practices: careful retries for transient failures, timeouts on everything, and budgets that bound the worst case.
body:
1. How agent runs fail, and who handles what

FailureExamplesHandler
Transient infrastructureModel API 429 with retry-after, 500, 504, 529; network resets; tool timeoutsRetry in code with backoff, jitter and caps
Persistent request error400 invalid request, 401/403 auth, 413 too large, spend-cap 429 without retry-afterDo not retry; fix the request or escalate
Tool error the model can fixUnknown id, bad date format, permission denied with an alternativeReturn as an error observation (ag2, ag3)
Process failureWorker crash, out-of-memory, deploy, host lossDurable journal and resume
Slow external dependencyHuman approval, long batch job, webhookPersist and wait without holding resources; resume on event
Runaway behaviourLoops, endless retries, exploding contextBudgets and no-progress detection (ag2)

The classification decides everything else. Anthropic's API documentation (checked 6 October 2026) lists the error types: 400 invalid_request_error, 401 authentication, 402 billing, 403 permission, 404 not found, 409 conflict, 413 request too large, 429 rate_limit_error, 500 api_error, 504 timeout and 529 overloaded_error. It recommends exponential backoff for 500s and notes that a 429 caused by a tier spend cap has no retry-after header and keeps failing. Its SDKs retry connection errors, 429s and 5xx errors twice by default with exponential backoff, honouring retry-after. Know what your client library already does before adding your own retries on top, or you will multiply them.

2. Retries done right

A retry is safe when the failure is transient and the operation is idempotent (or keyed). Then three questions remain: how long to wait, how many times, and how to avoid making things worse.

Exponential backoff waits longer after each failure. Temporal's default activity retry policy is a clean reference: initial interval 1 second, backoff coefficient 2.0, maximum interval 100 times the initial interval (100 seconds), unlimited attempts, and the wait before each retry is the smaller of initial × coefficientretries and the maximum. The schedule is:

Retry12345678910
Wait (s)1248163264100100100

Ten retries wait 427 seconds in total, and with unlimited attempts the activity keeps trying every 100 seconds until a timeout stops it. That suits infrastructure blips in background work. For a model call in an interactive agent, where a user is waiting, cap the attempts (perhaps 3-5) or set an overall deadline, and surface the failure.

Jitter randomises each wait (for example, a random value between zero and the computed backoff, "full jitter"). Without it, every client that failed at the same instant retries at the same instant, producing synchronised spikes that can keep a recovering service down.

Honour retry-after when the server provides it: it knows better than your formula when capacity will return.

Retry budgets cap retries as a fraction of normal traffic, say 10%, across a client or a fleet. During a provider incident, a fleet sending 1,000 requests per second with three immediate retries per failure and a 30% failure rate would add 900 requests per second of retries (1,000 × 0.3 × 3), nearly doubling the load on a service that is already failing. A 10% budget caps the extra at 100 per second.

Circuit breakers stop calling a dependency that is failing consistently: after the error rate passes a threshold, calls fail fast for a cooling-off period, then a few test calls decide whether to close the breaker. For agents, an open breaker on a model endpoint can trigger fallback to another region, provider or model. Fallback models must be evaluated in advance on the same tasks, because a different model is a different agent (ag12).

3. Timeouts at every level

Every external call needs a timeout, or a single hung connection can stall a run indefinitely. Timeouts nest:

  • Per attempt: for a model call, a time-to-first-token limit and an overall limit matched to the expected output length; Anthropic recommends streaming or the Batch API for requests that might exceed 10 minutes, since idle connections can be dropped. For a tool call, a limit from its latency profile (p99 plus margin).
  • Per operation across retries: the total time allowed including all attempts and backoff.
  • Heartbeats for long tools: a tool that runs for minutes reports progress periodically; if heartbeats stop, the system knows the worker died rather than waiting for the full timeout.
  • Per step and per run: deadlines that bound everything beneath them.

Temporal names these precisely, which makes it a useful vocabulary even if you do not use it. Start-To-Close limits one attempt of an activity; Schedule-To-Close limits the whole activity including retries; Schedule-To-Start limits how long a task may wait for a worker (detecting a starved fleet); and Heartbeat timeout detects silent failure of long activities. The documentation requires at least one of Start-To-Close or Schedule-To-Close and strongly recommends Start-To-Close, because the server relies on it to retry an attempt whose worker vanished. The design rule is arithmetic: per-attempt timeout × attempts + total backoff must fit inside the operation's limit, and operations must fit inside the step and run deadlines, or the outer deadline will cut retries short unpredictably.

4. The journal: record before you proceed

A durable agent appends to a journal before each next action. The entries, in order:

{"run": "r-7f3", "seq": 41, "type": "model_response", "step": 14, "content": [...], "usage": {...}}
{"run": "r-7f3", "seq": 42, "type": "tool_call", "step": 14, "tool": "crm_create",
 "args": {...}, "idempotency_key": "r-7f3:14:0"}
{"run": "r-7f3", "seq": 43, "type": "tool_result", "step": 14, "ok": true, "result": {...}}
{"run": "r-7f3", "seq": 44, "type": "budget", "steps": 14, "usd": 1.83, "input_tokens": 412000}
{"run": "r-7f3", "seq": 45, "type": "approval_request", "step": 15, "action": {...}}

On resume, a new worker loads the journal, rebuilds the message history and state, and walks forward. Steps with recorded results are replayed: their model responses and tool results come from the journal; nothing is called. The first step without a recorded result is where real work resumes. If its tool call was recorded as sent (seq 42) but has no result (no seq 43), the worker retries it with the same idempotency key, or for tools without keys, first checks whether the effect already happened.

Why record model responses rather than call the model again? Because the model is non-deterministic: called again with the same history, it may choose a different action. The run that already happened chose crm_create at step 14; a resumed run that chose crm_update instead would diverge from reality, and every later step would be built on a world that does not exist. The journal, not the model, is the source of truth about what has happened. It also makes runs reproducible for debugging and evaluation (ag12, ag14), and it is where prompt-cache-friendly append-only history (ag5) comes from naturally.

5. Durable execution engines: workflows and activities

Building journals, replay, timers and retries by hand is possible (hd7's platform does it on a database), but durable-execution engines package the pattern. Temporal is the best-known open-source example, and its model maps cleanly onto agents.

Code is split in two. A workflow is orchestration code that must be deterministic: given the same history, it must issue the same commands in the same order. Its progress is recorded as an event history, and after a crash the engine re-runs the workflow code against the history, a process called replay, to rebuild its state. Anything non-deterministic (network calls, clocks, random numbers) is forbidden inline; Temporal's documentation says to put such work in activities, which "execute outside the replay path and are automatically retried", or to use the SDK's replay-safe APIs for time and randomness. If code changes make replay issue different commands from the history, the engine raises a non-determinism error.

An agent loop maps onto this directly:

@workflow
def agent_run(task, budget):
    state = init_state(task, budget)
    while not state.done:
        check_budget(state)                                  # deterministic
        resp = call_activity(call_model, state.request(),    # recorded in history
                             retry=model_retry, timeout=model_timeout)
        state.append(resp)
        for call in resp.tool_calls:
            if needs_approval(call):
                decision = wait_for_signal("approval", call.id, timeout=hours(24))
                if not decision.approved: state.append_denied(call); continue
            result = call_activity(run_tool, call,
                                   key=f"{run_id()}:{state.step}:{call.index}",
                                   retry=tool_retry(call.tool), timeout=tool_timeout(call.tool))
            state.append(result)
        if state.history_too_long(): continue_as_new(state.compacted())

Model calls and tool calls are activities, each with a retry policy and timeouts; their results land in the event history, so replay reuses them and the model is never asked twice. Human approvals arrive as signals; waiting for one holds no worker, just a durable timer. Budgets are workflow state, so they survive restarts. Event histories have limits (51,200 events or 50 MB per execution, with warnings at 10,240 events or 10 MB, per Temporal's documentation), so a very long agent uses Continue-As-New to end the execution and start a fresh one carrying a compacted state, which pairs naturally with ag5's compaction. Large payloads, such as long model responses or tool results, are best stored externally with references in the history.

6. Idempotent side effects, check-then-act and sagas

Across a network, a request whose response was lost may or may not have been executed. Exactly-once execution is therefore impossible to guarantee from the client side; what is achievable is effectively-once: deliver at least once, and make repeats harmless. Three techniques, in order of preference:

  • Idempotency keys (ag3): send a key that identifies the intended operation; the server stores it with the result and returns the stored result for repeats. Derive it from the run and step (r-7f3:14:0) or from a business key, never from the attempt.
  • Check-then-act: for systems without key support, look up whether the effect already happened (does a record with this external reference exist?) before retrying. This has a race window, so pair it with a natural unique constraint where possible.
  • Naturally idempotent operations: prefer "set status to closed" over "toggle status", "upsert by external id" over "create".

Multi-step side effects need a saga: a sequence of steps where each completed step has a compensating action that semantically undoes it. Booking a trip: reserve the flight (compensation: cancel), reserve the hotel (compensation: cancel), charge the card (compensation: refund). If the hotel fails permanently after the flight succeeded, run the flight's compensation. Compensations are themselves side effects, so they too are keyed, retried and journalled. Where an action cannot be compensated (an email cannot be unsent), place it last, or put a reservation or confirmation step before it.

7. Budgets that survive

Budgets bound the worst case. Per run: steps, input and output tokens, money, wall-clock time, and per-tool call counts (ag2). Per user and per tenant: daily or monthly quotas. Fleet-wide: a global spend rate with alerts. Three engineering rules make them real:

  • Durable: budget counters are part of the run's journalled state, updated in the same write as the step they account for. A counter in memory resets on every restart, which is exactly when runaway runs restart most.
  • Checked before spending: the orchestrator checks the remaining budget before each model or tool call, including estimating the call's cost (input tokens are known before sending).
  • Graceful at the limit: on exhaustion, stop cleanly, record which budget ran out, ask the model for a brief handover summary with a small reserved allowance, and escalate or return a partial result. A run that simply dies leaves no trace of how far it got.

8. The cost of restarting from scratch, worked

How much does durability matter? Model interruptions (deploys, crashes, host losses) as random events arriving at an average interval of M hours, and a task that needs T hours of uninterrupted work. If any interruption sends the task back to the start, the expected total time is M(eT/M − 1), a standard result for restarts under exponentially distributed failures. With M = 6 hours:

Task length TP(interrupted at least once)Expected time, restart from scratchMultiplier
1 hour15%1.09 h1.09×
3 hours39%3.89 h1.30×
6 hours63%10.3 h1.72×

The multiplier grows exponentially with task length, and cost (tokens, sandbox time) grows with it. With per-step checkpoints, an interruption costs about one step plus the resume overhead, so the multiplier stays close to 1 at any length. And the table understates the problem, because restarts also repeat non-idempotent side effects and may take different paths, which no multiplier captures. For runs of minutes, checkpointing is good hygiene; for runs of hours, it is the difference between a product and a demo.
deep:
Why replay needs recorded model outputs

Classic durable execution assumes deterministic orchestration and non-deterministic activities. Agents make the orchestration itself depend on a non-deterministic component: the next action is chosen by a model. The resolution is to treat each model call as an activity, so its output is recorded, and to make the code that reacts to that output deterministic. Then replay is faithful: the same recorded outputs lead to the same decisions. Two subtleties follow. Changing the prompt-building code between a crash and a resume changes what would have been sent, but replay does not send it again, so the resumed run's earlier context reflects the old code; that is correct, since it reflects what the model actually saw. And sampling parameters, model versions and tool definitions belong in the journal too, so a run can be explained later.

Workflow versioning

Durable runs outlive deploys. If version 8 of the orchestration code makes different decisions at a point where version 7's run is paused, replaying version 7's history under version 8's code produces a non-determinism error or, worse, a silent divergence. Durable engines provide versioning mechanisms (marking code paths with version branches so old histories take old branches), and platforms can run old and new workers side by side until old runs drain. Anthropic's description of rainbow deployments for its research agents is the same idea at the deployment level. The minimum discipline is to store the code version in each run, keep schemas backward compatible, and test resuming the previous release's journals in CI.

Poison pills and quarantine

Some runs fail every time: a document that crashes the parser, a state that triggers a bug, a tool call that times out deterministically. With unlimited retries and automatic resume, such a run can consume workers forever and starve others. Detect repeated failures of the same run or step (by count and by fingerprint of the error), stop retrying, move the run to a quarantine state with its journal intact, and alert. A person can inspect, fix and resume it, or abandon it with an explanation to the user.

Backpressure and fairness

Model providers enforce rate limits per organisation, typically in requests and tokens per minute. A fleet of agents that ignores them gets 429s; one that respects them needs a shared view of capacity. Token-bucket limiters per model endpoint, per tenant quotas so one customer's batch of long runs cannot starve others, and queues that admit new runs only when capacity exists are standard. Durable runs make this easier: a run that cannot get capacity can wait cheaply, parked, rather than spinning.

Hedged requests trade cost for tail latency

For latency-sensitive steps, a client can send a second identical request if the first has not responded within, say, the 95th-percentile latency, and use whichever finishes first. This cuts tail latency substantially at the cost of extra calls (bounded by how often the hedge fires). For model calls it doubles the cost of the hedged fraction and can return different outputs; it should be used only for idempotent, read-only calls, only for a small tail, and with the losing call cancelled. ag13 returns to the latency-cost trade-off.

Mid-stream failures

Streaming responses fail differently: the server can return HTTP 200 and then send an error event partway through, after some output has arrived. Anthropic's documentation notes that such errors do not follow the standard error mechanisms. A durable loop should treat a partial streamed response as a failed attempt (never journal half a tool call as the model's response) and retry the whole call, which is another reason for idempotent tools: a partial stream must never trigger an action.

Test failure, not just success

Reliability machinery is only trustworthy if it has been exercised. Chaos testing for agents means, in staging: killing workers at random points within steps (especially between sending a tool call and recording its result); injecting provider errors and latency; making tools hang; and deploying new versions while runs are in flight. The assertions are concrete: every run completes or stops with a recorded reason, no side effect is duplicated, budgets hold across restarts, and resumed runs make the same decisions the journal says they made.

Durability does not replace correctness

A durable runtime guarantees the run continues; it does not guarantee the run is right. A model that misread the task at step 3 will, after a perfectly faithful replay, continue to act on the misreading. Durability should be paired with verification (ag1, ag2) and with the ability for a person to inspect a run mid-flight, correct its state or plan, and resume, which a journal makes possible and a pure in-memory loop does not.
prod:
The case: durable execution in practice (Temporal) and resumable agents (Anthropic)

Temporal's documentation captures the general pattern this lesson applies to agents. Activities carry retry policies whose default (1-second initial interval, doubling, capped at 100 seconds, unlimited attempts) is tuned for infrastructure faults; workflows do not retry by default, because a workflow failure usually means a bug or a business decision rather than a blip. Timeouts are explicit and layered (Schedule-To-Start, Start-To-Close, Schedule-To-Close, Heartbeat), with Start-To-Close strongly recommended because the server relies on it to recover from lost workers. Workflow code must be deterministic so the event history can be replayed, and non-deterministic work belongs in activities. Histories have limits (51,200 events or 50 MB) and very long executions continue as new. Each of these is a direct answer to a failure in the opening story: lost progress, synchronised retries, hung calls, and runs that grow without bound.

Anthropic's account of operating its multi-agent research system shows the same lessons arriving from the agent side. The post notes that in long-running stateful agents, minor system failures can be catastrophic because errors compound, so the team built the ability to resume from where the agent was when an error occurred rather than restarting, combined model-driven adaptation (letting the agent know a tool failed so it can work around it) with deterministic safeguards such as retry logic and regular checkpoints, added full production tracing to diagnose non-deterministic failures, and used rainbow deployments so that updates did not break agents mid-run.

Failure modes and their signatures

Duplicate side effects: two records, two emails, two charges for one intent; missing or per-attempt idempotency keys. Lost runs: runs that vanish on deploys; state in memory, not journalled. Divergent resumes: resumed runs that redo or contradict earlier steps; the model was re-called during replay. Retry amplification: request volume to a provider spikes during its incident; no jitter, no budget, retries stacked across layers (SDK plus your code plus a gateway). Budget leaks: runs exceeding limits after restarts; counters not durable. Stuck runs: runs waiting forever on a tool with no timeout or heartbeat. Poison pills: the same run crashing workers repeatedly.

What to monitor

Retry rates by error class and dependency; circuit-breaker state changes; requests per second including retries versus first attempts; resumes per run and the step at which they occurred; replay duration; duplicate operations prevented by idempotency keys (a healthy non-zero number shows the keys are working); budget exhaustion by type; time spent waiting on approvals and external events; quarantined runs; and event-history size per run against limits.

Knobs

Retry policies per dependency (initial interval, coefficient, cap, attempts, non-retryable errors); retry budget fraction; breaker thresholds and fallback targets; timeouts per attempt, operation, step and run; heartbeat intervals for long tools; journal granularity; Continue-As-New thresholds; budget limits per run, user and tenant; quarantine thresholds. Tune them from incident reviews and chaos testing: kill workers mid-step, inject provider errors and slow tools in staging, and check that runs resume correctly with no duplicate effects.
myths: Retrying failed calls always improves reliability.

Retries help only for transient failures and only for operations that are safe to repeat. Retrying a 400 invalid-request error wastes time; retrying a non-idempotent payment can charge twice; and synchronised retries from many clients during a provider incident multiply load and prolong the outage. Retries need classification, idempotency, backoff with jitter, caps and a retry budget.
If the process crashes, just re-run the agent from the start.

Re-running from the start repeats every side effect that was not idempotent, burns all the tokens again, and may take a different path because model outputs vary. For long runs it is also expensive: with interruptions every six hours on average, a six-hour task restarted from scratch costs about 1.72 times as much on expectation. Durable runs record progress and resume.
Saving the conversation history is enough to resume.

You also need the state of every in-flight side effect (was the email sent before the crash?), the budget counters, pending approvals and the plan. And you must reuse the recorded model responses rather than calling the model again on replay, or the resumed run may diverge from what was already done. A journal of model responses, tool calls with idempotency keys and results, and approvals is what makes resumption faithful.
Exactly-once execution of tool calls is achievable with enough care.

Across a network, a request whose response was lost may or may not have been executed, and no amount of client care can tell. What is achievable is effectively-once: at-least-once delivery plus idempotent handling (or a status check before retry), so that repeats have no additional effect.
Budgets are a cost feature, not a reliability feature.

Budgets are how a system fails safely when something unexpected happens: a loop, a confused model, a slow tool, a provider that keeps erroring. A run without enforced step, token, money and time limits is a run whose worst case is unbounded.
