t: Agent interoperability protocols: MCP, A2A and what else is real (as of Oct 2026)
sum: What each protocol solves: MCP for agent-to-tools (recap) versus A2A 1.0 for agent-to-agent, with agent cards, tasks and their eight states, messages, parts, artifacts, streaming and push worked on the wire; AG-UI and AP2 around them; discovery, auth and trust between vendors; failure, retry and timeout semantics; and when you should not split a system into communicating agents.
prereq: ag4

MCP connects a host application to servers that expose tools, resources and prompts over JSON-RPC, using stdio or Streamable HTTP; the 2026-07-28 revision is stateless, and remote servers use OAuth 2.1.
ag8

Multi-agent systems split work between an orchestrator and workers or hand off between agents; they pay off only when work parallelises or needs isolated context, and they multiply cost and failure modes.
ag10
Content from outside the system, including another agent's output, can carry prompt injection; an agent with private data, untrusted input and an outbound channel can be made to leak.
ag11
Reliable agents use timeouts, retries with backoff, idempotency keys for side effects, checkpoints and budgets.
au12
Agents acting for users need delegated, scoped credentials (for example via OAuth token exchange), with every call authorised and audited.
net11
Server-Sent Events stream events over one HTTP response; webhooks push events by calling a URL the receiver registered.
why:
A travel company builds an agent that plans business trips. It is good at understanding what a traveller wants, but the actual inventory lives elsewhere: airlines, hotel chains and a corporate-card provider each run their own agents, built on different frameworks, by different teams, behind different security perimeters. The travel agent cannot call their internal tools, and they would never let it. What it can do is ask: "book a refundable seat on a morning flight to Berlin under this fare policy", and let the airline's agent decide how. Without a shared protocol, every pair of companies negotiates a custom integration, with its own way of describing what an agent can do, tracking a job that takes twenty minutes, asking a clarifying question, proving who is calling, and reporting the result. With five partners that is five integrations; with fifty it is a full-time team.

This is the problem interoperability protocols address, and in 2025–26 two became widely adopted. The Model Context Protocol (MCP, ag4) standardised how an agent uses tools and data: one agent, many capabilities it drives directly. Agent2Agent (A2A) standardised how one agent delegates a task to another, independent agent: opaque collaborators, long-running work, clarifying questions, artifacts. Around them, smaller protocols cover the edges: AG-UI for streaming an agent's work to a user interface, and AP2 for proving a user authorised a payment. The field moves monthly, so every claim in this lesson about versions and adoption is dated.

Senior interviews probe this with "MCP or A2A, and why?", "how would two companies' agents trust each other?", "what happens when the remote agent times out halfway through a booking?" and, most usefully, "would you even split this into multiple agents?". Good answers know what each protocol standardises and, just as important, what it leaves to you: semantics, trust, failure handling and the decision not to add a network hop.

This lesson recaps MCP briefly, then works through A2A 1.0 in detail: agent cards and discovery, tasks and their states, messages, parts and artifacts, the operations and their three wire bindings, streaming and push notifications, and versioning. It covers authentication and trust between vendors, failure and timeout semantics, the other protocols with real adoption on the day of writing, and the architecture question of when not to use any of them. The lab builds a toy two-agent exchange over a JSON task protocol in the standard library.

A note on what "agent-to-agent" means in practice today. Most production traffic between agents in 2026 is still between agents owned by one organisation, often over plain APIs or a framework's own conventions, and the cross-company A2A deployments the Linux Foundation describes are concentrated in areas like supply chain, financial services, insurance and IT operations, where many independent parties already exchange structured work. So the skill interviewers test is less "recite the A2A spec" and more "know when a protocol boundary is warranted, what it gives you, and what you still have to build around it".
primer:
Tools you drive versus contractors you hire

Think about how a building company works. Some things it does with its own tools: a drill, a ladder, a measuring tape. It decides exactly what each tool does and when, and the tool returns immediately. Other things it hires out: the electrical work goes to a licensed electrician. The builder does not tell the electrician which wire to cut; it describes the job ("wire the kitchen to code, budget £3,000"), the electrician plans the work with their own tools, may come back with questions ("do you want under-cabinet lighting?"), takes days, and hands over a certificate at the end. The builder needs a way to find electricians, check their licences, track the job, answer questions and receive the result, but never sees inside the electrician's van.

MCP is the standard for tools: an agent sees each tool's name, description and input schema and calls it with arguments of its choosing. A2A is the standard for hiring contractors: an agent finds another agent by its published Agent Card, sends a task in natural language and structured parts, tracks it through states, answers questions when the remote agent needs input, and receives artifacts. The remote agent is opaque: its prompts, tools, model and memory are its own business.

The analogy breaks in one way that matters for security: a human contractor is unlikely to be talked into stealing from you by a note left in your kitchen, while an agent can be manipulated by content it reads. Messages from a remote agent are untrusted input to your own model, however reputable the vendor.

The protocol stack around an agent

What a protocol can and cannot standardise

A protocol can standardise the envelope: how to find an agent, how to describe what it offers, how to start, track, question, cancel and finish a piece of work, how to authenticate, how to signal errors and versions. It cannot standardise meaning. When the travel agent asks the airline agent for "a refundable morning flight", the two must agree on what refundable and morning mean, which details are required, and what a good answer looks like. Skills in an Agent Card are described in natural language, with tags and examples; whether the remote agent really does what its card says is learned by testing, contracts and experience. Keep that limit in mind: interoperability protocols remove plumbing work, not integration judgement.

A short history, because versions matter

MCP was open-sourced by Anthropic in late 2024 and adopted quickly by AI platforms and developer tools; by the time the Linux Foundation formed the Agentic AI Foundation around it in December 2025, the foundation counted over 10,000 MCP servers. A2A was announced by Google in April 2025 with about 50 partners, donated to the Linux Foundation in June 2025, went through 0.2 and 0.3 releases during 2025, and reached 1.0 in March 2026. Interviewers sometimes test whether you know these are recent and still moving: an answer that says "as of the 1.0 specification" or "in the 2026-07-28 MCP revision" shows you know which version you are describing, and that you would check before building on a detail.

A reader who stops here should remember: MCP is for tools you control, A2A is for other agents you delegate to, both are envelopes, and every protocol hop is a cost you should only pay at a real boundary.
body:
1. What problem each protocol solves

MCPA2A
ConnectsAn agent (host) to tool and data serversAn agent (client) to another agent (remote server)
Unit of interactionA tool call with typed arguments, a resource read, a promptA task: a goal plus messages, tracked through states
Who decides howThe calling agent chooses tool and argumentsThe remote agent plans and acts on its own
DurationUsually secondsSeconds to hours; can pause for input or authorisation
VisibilityTool schemas and results are in the caller's contextRemote internals are opaque; only messages and artifacts
Typical boundaryInside your system, or a vendor's tool APIBetween teams or organisations
GovernanceAgentic AI Foundation (Linux Foundation), since Dec 2025Linux Foundation project, contributed by Google in June 2025

A rule of thumb follows. If you would describe the interaction as "call this function", it is a tool, and MCP (or a plain API) fits. If you would describe it as "get this done and tell me when it's finished", and the other side has its own judgement, state and owners, it is a task for another agent, and A2A fits.

2. MCP in one paragraph

As covered in ag4: an MCP host (the agent application) runs clients that connect to servers; servers expose tools (callable functions with JSON Schema inputs), resources (readable data) and prompts (templates). Messages are JSON-RPC over stdio for local servers or Streamable HTTP for remote ones; the 2026-07-28 revision made the protocol stateless; remote servers use OAuth 2.1 authorisation. Tool names, descriptions and results all land in the model's context, which is why tool descriptions are prompt surface and why MCP servers are supply-chain dependencies. Nothing in this lesson changes that; A2A sits beside it.

3. A2A's building blocks

A2A, in its 1.0 specification (released 12 March 2026; 1.0.1 on 28 May 2026), defines a small data model.

  • Agent Card: the remote agent's self-description, a JSON document with its name and description, a list of supported interfaces (each a URL, a protocol binding and a protocol version), the provider organisation, capabilities (streaming, push notifications, extended card), security schemes and requirements, default input and output media types, and skills.
  • Skill: one capability, with an id, a name, a natural-language description, tags, example requests and accepted input and output types.
  • Message: one turn, with a role (user or agent), a messageId, optional taskId and contextId, and parts.
  • Part: the smallest unit of content: text, a file reference, or structured data.
  • Task: the stateful unit of work, with an id, a contextId, a status (state plus an optional agent message), a history and artifacts.
  • Artifact: an output of the task, made of parts: a document, an image, a JSON result.
  • Context: an id grouping related tasks and messages into one conversation.

A shortened Agent Card, modelled on the specification's example:

{
  "name": "Invoice Checker",
  "description": "Validates supplier invoices against purchase orders.",
  "supportedInterfaces": [
    {"url": "https://agents.supplier.example/a2a/v1", "protocolBinding": "JSONRPC", "protocolVersion": "1.0"}
  ],
  "provider": {"organization": "Supplier Example Ltd", "url": "https://supplier.example"},
  "version": "2.3.0",
  "capabilities": {"streaming": true, "pushNotifications": true, "extendedAgentCard": true},
  "securitySchemes": {"oidc": {"openIdConnectSecurityScheme":
      {"openIdConnectUrl": "https://login.supplier.example/.well-known/openid-configuration"}}},
  "securityRequirements": [{"schemes": {"oidc": {"list": ["invoices.read"]}}}],
  "defaultInputModes": ["application/json", "text/plain"],
  "defaultOutputModes": ["application/json"],
  "skills": [{"id": "check-invoice", "name": "Check an invoice",
              "description": "Checks totals, tax and PO match; asks for the PO number if missing.",
              "tags": ["finance", "invoices"], "examples": ["Check invoice INV-77 against its PO"]}],
  "signatures": [{"protected": "eyJhbGciOiJFUzI1NiIs…", "signature": "QFdkNLNs…"}]
}

4. Discovery

Clients find Agent Cards in three ways, per the specification: a well-known URI, https://{domain}/.well-known/agent-card.json; registries or catalogues that curate cards; and direct configuration. The well-known path makes the domain the anchor of identity: if TLS proves you are talking to supplier.example, the card served there is the one that domain publishes. Cards can be cached (the specification gives guidance) but must be refreshed, because interfaces, versions and skills change. Details an agent does not want to publish can go in an extended Agent Card, returned only to authenticated clients through GetExtendedAgentCard.

A2A 1.0 lets a card carry signatures: JSON Web Signatures (RFC 7515) over the card's content after canonicalising it with the JSON Canonicalization Scheme (RFC 8785), so any client can check that the card was published by the holder of a given key, even if it was obtained from a registry rather than the agent's own domain. A signature proves origin and integrity, not good behaviour.

5. The task lifecycle

A task moves through eight states. Four are active: submitted (accepted, not started), working, input-required (the agent needs something from the client to continue, with a message explaining what) and auth-required (the agent needs additional authorisation, such as the end user's consent to access their account). Four are terminal: completed, failed, canceled and rejected (the agent declined the task). Once a task is terminal it accepts no more messages; a follow-up becomes a new task in the same context.

6. Operations and wire bindings

A2A 1.0 defines eleven operations abstractly and maps each to three bindings (JSON-RPC, gRPC and HTTP+JSON/REST) that must behave identically:

OperationJSON-RPC methodREST endpoint
Send messageSendMessagePOST /message:send
Send streaming messageSendStreamingMessagePOST /message:stream
Get taskGetTaskGET /tasks/{id}
List tasksListTasksGET /tasks
Cancel taskCancelTaskPOST /tasks/{id}:cancel
Subscribe to taskSubscribeToTaskPOST /tasks/{id}:subscribe
Push-notification config (create, get, list, delete)…TaskPushNotificationConfig/tasks/{id}/pushNotificationConfigs
Get extended Agent CardGetExtendedAgentCardGET /extendedAgentCard

A send over the REST binding, from the specification's basic example:

POST /message:send HTTP/1.1
Host: agent.example.com
Content-Type: application/a2a+json
A2A-Version: 1.0
Authorization: Bearer …

{"message": {"role": "ROLE_USER", "messageId": "msg-uuid",
             "parts": [{"text": "What is the weather today?"}]}}

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
{"task": {"id": "task-uuid", "contextId": "context-uuid",
          "status": {"state": "TASK_STATE_COMPLETED"},
          "artifacts": [{"artifactId": "artifact-uuid", "name": "Weather Report",
                         "parts": [{"text": "Today will be sunny with a high of 75°F"}]}]}}

SendMessage returns immediately with either a direct Message (for simple interactions) or a Task; with return_immediately unset, it waits until the task reaches a terminal state, and with it set to true it returns as soon as the task is created. Errors map to binding-specific codes: for example TaskNotFoundError is JSON-RPC −32001 and HTTP 404, TaskNotCancelableError −32002, UnsupportedOperationError −32004 and VersionNotSupportedError −32009.

7. Streaming, push notifications and polling

Three ways to follow a long task. Streaming: SendStreamingMessage (or SubscribeToTask for an existing task) returns a stream, over SSE in the HTTP bindings, that begins with the Task object and continues with TaskStatusUpdateEvent and TaskArtifactUpdateEvent objects until the task ends. It suits a client that is online and wants live progress. Push notifications: the client registers a webhook URL for the task; the agent POSTs status and artifact updates to it. It suits tasks that run for minutes or hours, and server-to-server integrations where nobody holds a connection open. The specification tells clients to process notifications idempotently because duplicates may be delivered, and the agent must only send to URLs it is willing to call, since a webhook URL supplied by a client is a classic server-side request forgery vector. Polling: GetTask at intervals, simplest and the universal fallback after a reconnect.

8. Versioning

A2A identifies protocol versions by major.minor (1.0); patch releases do not change compatibility. Clients must send an A2A-Version header (or request parameter) on every request; agents must process the request using that version's semantics or return VersionNotSupportedError. An empty header is treated as 0.3, so pre-1.0 clients continue to work with agents that still support 0.3. An agent can advertise several interfaces with different versions in its card, which lets providers migrate clients gradually. The A2A 1.0 release also introduced multi-tenancy features, modernised security flows and signed cards, according to the Linux Foundation's announcement.

9. Authentication, authorisation and trust between vendors

Trust has layers, and A2A provides hooks for each rather than a single answer.

  • Server identity: TLS on the agent's domain, plus a signed Agent Card if you obtained it elsewhere.
  • Client authentication: the card's security schemes say what the agent accepts (OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, API keys and others); the client obtains credentials out of band and presents them on each request. The specification is explicit that identity is established at the transport layer, not inside message content.
  • Authorisation: the remote agent must authorise every operation and only show a client the tasks it may see. For actions on a user's behalf, use delegated, scoped credentials (au12) rather than a powerful shared key.
  • In-task authorisation: if mid-task the agent needs more permission, such as a user's consent to read their bank data, it moves the task to auth-required and the client resolves it, possibly by asking its own caller, all the way up to a human. The specification warns that this state change by itself authorises nothing; credentials obtained for one request must not be assumed to cover later ones.
  • Behavioural trust: none of the above proves the remote agent does what its card says, handles your data well or resists manipulation. That comes from contracts, security reviews, testing, monitoring and limiting exposure: send the minimum data a task needs, validate artifacts against schemas, and treat every message from the remote agent as untrusted content for your model (ag10).

10. Failure and timeout semantics

Distributed tasks fail in partial ways, and A2A gives you the vocabulary to handle them, not the policy.

Duplicate sends. If the network fails after you send, you do not know whether the task was created. Retry with the same messageId; the specification allows agents to use it to detect duplicates, so check that your partner's agent does, and make your own A2A server do so. Get and list operations are naturally idempotent; cancel is idempotent.

Deadlines. The protocol has no global timeout. Set your own deadline per task, based on what your caller can tolerate, and when it expires send CancelTask, then read the task's final state. Cancel is a request: the agent may answer TaskNotCancelableError or may already have done irreversible work. Anything with side effects (a booking, a payment) needs idempotency keys and a compensating action on the remote side.

Stalls. A task in input-required or auth-required waits for you indefinitely unless you time it out. Decide who answers questions (your agent, your user) and how long you wait.

Partial results. Artifacts can stream in before a task fails; decide whether partial results are usable, and mark them.

Disconnects. If a stream drops, resubscribe or poll; if your webhook was down, list tasks by context and state to catch up.

Version and capability errors. Check the card's capabilities before using streaming or push; handle VersionNotSupportedError by negotiating an interface you both support.

11. The other protocols with real adoption

On 9 October 2026, beyond MCP and A2A, three adjacent efforts had visible adoption. AG-UI, the Agent-User Interaction Protocol from the CopilotKit community, is an open, event-based protocol for connecting agents to user-facing applications: messages, tool calls and state changes streamed to a front end so any compliant UI can render any compliant agent. AP2, the Agent Payments Protocol from Google's agentic-commerce effort, extends A2A with cryptographically signed mandates that record a user's authorisation for a purchase; the Linux Foundation's April 2026 announcement counted more than 60 supporting organisations in payments and financial services. And commerce-specific protocols (such as UCP, which the same announcement describes as compatible with AP2 mandates) sit on top for shopping flows. On governance, MCP moved to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation when it was formed on 9 December 2025, alongside Block's goose and OpenAI's AGENTS.md; A2A is a separate Linux Foundation project. Names and positions in this space change quickly; check the projects' pages before relying on any of them.

12. When not to split into communicating agents

Interoperability protocols make it easy to build systems out of many agents, which makes it easy to build systems that are slower, costlier and less reliable than they need to be. Each A2A hop adds a network round trip and authentication, serialises context into messages (losing whatever the remote side is not told), runs another model with its own errors, and adds a partial-failure mode. Reliability multiplies: if each hop succeeds 95% of the time, a chain of five succeeds 0.95⁵ ≈ 77% of the time. Latency adds: five hops of a few seconds each is a long wait.

So the default inside one team, one codebase and one trust domain is not A2A. Use tools for capabilities, plain function calls or in-process sub-agents for decomposition (ag8), and a single agent where one will do. Reach for A2A when there is a real boundary: another organisation, another team that owns and deploys its agent independently, a different security or compliance domain, or a capability you buy rather than build. Even then, ask whether a plain API (deterministic, testable, cheap) would serve better than an agent; A2A is for when the other side genuinely needs judgement and conversation.

13. A delegation, end to end

Put the pieces together with the travel example. The trip-planning agent needs a refundable morning flight to Berlin for an employee.

  1. Discovery (once, cached): it fetches https://agents.airline.example/.well-known/agent-card.json, verifies the card's JWS signature against the airline's published key, sees a JSON-RPC interface at protocol version 1.0, a book-flight skill, streaming and push support, and an OAuth 2.0 scheme requiring a bookings scope.
  2. Credentials: it obtains a token for the corporate account, scoped to bookings for this traveller, through the company's identity provider (token exchange, au12).
  3. Send (t = 0): SendStreamingMessage with a messageId stored against the trip request, a text part with the goal and a data part with structured constraints (date, cabin, fare rules, cost centre). The stream opens with a Task in state working.
  4. Clarification (t ≈ 9 s): a status update moves the task to input-required: "Two refundable options: 07:10 at €412 or 09:45 at €389. Which?" The planner checks the travel policy, picks the cheaper compliant option, and sends a message with the same taskId.
  5. Authorisation (t ≈ 14 s): the airline agent moves the task to auth-required because the fare exceeds the company's pre-approved limit for that route. The planner escalates to the employee's manager through its own UI; approval arrives after 6 minutes; the planner sends the approval reference.
  6. Completion (t ≈ 6 min 30 s): artifacts arrive (a booking record as structured data, an e-ticket as a file part) and the task ends in completed. The planner validates the booking data against its schema before telling the traveller.
  7. Failure path: had the stream dropped at step 4, the planner would resubscribe; had it hit its 15-minute deadline in auth-required, it would cancel, read the final state, and tell the traveller the booking was not made, or that it was made if the cancel came too late.

Notice where the protocol helped (finding the agent, the states, the clarifying turn, the authorisation pause, structured artifacts) and where your design did the work (credentials, policy, deadlines, validation, the human approval). That division is the whole lesson in one trace.

14. Choosing between MCP, A2A and a plain API, worked

Three integrations from one company's backlog show the decision. A currency-conversion service: deterministic, instant, schema-shaped; expose it as an MCP tool or call its API. A vendor's contract-review service that reads a contract, asks which jurisdiction applies, and returns a marked-up document after an hour of work by its own agent and lawyers: goal-shaped, long-running, conversational, owned by another company; A2A. An internal "summary agent" and "translation agent" that another team built inside the same product, called synchronously from one workflow: same codebase, same trust domain, same deploy cadence; make them functions or in-process sub-agents and skip the protocol. The questions behind each answer are always the same: is the other side deterministic or does it exercise judgement, is the work quick or long, and is there an ownership or trust boundary between us?
deep:
Opaqueness is a feature and a cost

A2A deliberately hides the remote agent's internals: its prompts, tools, model and memory. That protects the provider's intellectual property and security, lets it change implementation freely, and keeps your context small. The cost is that you cannot debug inside it, cannot inspect why it reached a decision, and cannot easily reproduce a failure. Plan for that asymmetry: ask partners for task-level logs or trace exports, insist on structured artifacts you can validate, and keep your own records of every message sent and received.

Semantic interoperability is the hard part

Two agents can speak A2A perfectly and still fail to cooperate because their skills mean different things. A skill described as "book travel" might expect an approved budget code; another expects a traveller profile id. Teams handle this with structured data parts that follow agreed JSON schemas for important skills, examples in the card that pin down expected inputs, contract tests run against the partner's agent in a sandbox, and A2A's extension mechanism for domain-specific conventions. The protocol's natural-language skills are a starting point for discovery, not a contract.

Why three bindings

JSON-RPC came first and matches MCP's style; gRPC suits high-throughput internal service meshes; HTTP+JSON fits existing API gateways, caching and tooling. A2A 1.0 requires functional equivalence across them, with an error-code mapping table, so an organisation can pick the binding that fits its infrastructure. The practical advice: pick one binding per integration, test it, and do not assume a partner supports all three; the card lists exactly what it offers.

Observability across organisations

When a task spans your agent and a vendor's, a slow or wrong answer has two halves. Correlate them with ids: the task and context ids A2A provides, plus your own trace id passed in message metadata or request headers if both sides agree to carry it. Record every state transition with timestamps in your traces (ag14), so you can say "the vendor's agent sat in working for 14 minutes" rather than "the booking was slow". Agree on retention and redaction of exchanged content, because traces of cross-company messages contain both companies' data.

Registries and the discovery problem

The well-known URI solves "what does this domain's agent offer?" but not "which agent should I use for this?". Organisations with many agents build registries: a catalogue of cards with ownership, environment, version, data classification and access policy, searched by skill and tags. The Linux Foundation's announcement lists registry consolidation on A2A's roadmap. Until a standard exists, treat your registry as a governance tool: it is where you enforce who may call which agent, verify signatures, and alert when a card changes.

Agents calling agents calling agents

Delegation chains compound every problem: latency, cost, reliability, and especially authority. If your agent delegates to a vendor's agent, which delegates to a subcontractor's, the user's permissions should narrow at each hop, not widen. A2A's auth-required state propagates authorisation requests up the chain to a human, and token exchange with narrowing scopes (au12) keeps each hop's authority minimal. Set a maximum delegation depth in policy; unbounded delegation is how small errors become expensive incidents.

Comparing with plain APIs

Many "agent-to-agent" integrations would be better as ordinary APIs: deterministic endpoints with schemas, versioning, rate limits and service-level agreements. Use A2A when the remote side must interpret goals, ask clarifying questions, or plan multi-step work under its own control. If the remote work is always the same function, an API is cheaper, faster, easier to test and easier to trust, and your agent can still call it as an MCP tool.

Testing integrations you do not control

With an opaque remote agent, testing shifts to the boundary. Maintain a contract-test suite per partner skill: representative requests with expected artifact schemas and properties, clarifying-question paths (does it ask for the PO number when missing?), refusal paths (does it reject out-of-scope tasks?), and failure paths (duplicate messageIds, cancellation mid-task, expired credentials). Run it against the partner's sandbox on a schedule and whenever their card changes. Because the remote agent is a model, run each case several times and track pass rates rather than single outcomes (ag12); a partner upgrade that drops a skill's pass rate from 98% to 85% is an incident even if nothing else changed.
prod:
The public case: A2A's first year (Linux Foundation, April 2026)

On 9 April 2026, the Linux Foundation reported on A2A's first year as a hosted project. Supporting organisations grew from more than 50 at launch in April 2025 to more than 150, including AWS, Cisco, Google, IBM, Microsoft, Salesforce, SAP and ServiceNow; the core repository passed 22,000 GitHub stars; and SDKs grew from one Python implementation to five production languages including JavaScript, Java, Go and .NET. Version 1.0, the first stable specification, added multi-protocol support, multi-tenancy, modernised security flows, signed Agent Cards and a migration path for early adopters. Cloud platforms embedded it: Microsoft in Azure AI Foundry and Copilot Studio, AWS in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. The announcement described production deployments in supply chain, financial services, insurance and IT operations, agents built on different frameworks (it names LangGraph and CrewAI) delegating sub-tasks without sharing memory, and AP2 extending A2A into payments with more than 60 organisations. It also stated the relationship plainly: A2A covers agents coordinating across organisational boundaries, MCP covers agents connecting to internal tools and data. Read it as the project's own account, with adoption numbers self-reported, but as evidence that A2A had moved from announcement to infrastructure.

Failure modes in practice

Duplicate side effects. A retry without the same messageId, or an agent that ignores it, creates two bookings. Test duplicate handling explicitly with every partner.

Zombie tasks. Tasks left in working or input-required forever because nobody owned the timeout. Sweep for non-terminal tasks older than their deadline.

Card drift. A partner changes a skill's behaviour or required inputs without changing its description. Pin card versions, diff cards on refresh, and run contract tests.

Webhook abuse. Push-notification URLs pointing at internal addresses, or unauthenticated webhooks accepting forged updates. Validate URLs, authenticate deliveries, and deduplicate.

Cross-agent injection. A partner's agent relays instructions from content it read. Treat its output as untrusted and keep it away from contexts with private data and outbound tools.

Unnecessary agents. Internal "microagents" talking A2A to each other inside one product, each hop adding seconds and failure modes. Collapse them.

What to monitor

Per partner agent and skill: task volume, state distribution and time in each state, terminal outcome rates (completed, failed, rejected, canceled), time to first artifact, duplicate-send rate, cancellations that did not stop work, version negotiation errors, authentication failures, and validation failures on artifacts. Alert on rising input-required stalls and on any change to a partner's Agent Card.

Operational practices that pay off

Keep an integration runbook per partner: contacts, escalation path, how to disable the integration quickly, and how to reconcile tasks with the partner's own records after an outage. Store every message and artifact you exchange, with redaction, for at least as long as the business process needs to be auditable. Version your own A2A server's card carefully: add skills and fields compatibly, announce removals in advance, and keep the previous protocol version's interface available while clients migrate. And track cost: a remote agent's work is often billed per task, so a retry storm or a looping clarification can cost real money on both sides.
myths: A2A replaces MCP.

They sit at different layers. MCP connects an agent to tools and data that it drives directly, function by function. A2A connects an agent to another agent that decides for itself how to do a task and may take minutes or hours. The A2A project describes the two as complementary, and many systems use both: an agent exposes itself over A2A and uses MCP servers internally.
If two agents speak A2A, they will work together.

A2A standardises the envelope: discovery, tasks, messages, states, auth hooks. It does not make two agents agree on what 'check an invoice' means, which inputs a skill needs, or what a good result is. Skills are described in natural language, so semantic mismatch, not wire format, is where integrations fail.
An agent card proves who you are talking to.

A card is the agent's own description of itself. TLS proves the server controls the domain, and A2A 1.0 lets cards be signed with JWS so you can verify who published them, but neither proves the agent behaves as described. Trust comes from contracts, verification, reputation and limiting what the remote agent can do to you.
Cancelling a task stops the work.

Cancel is a request. The remote agent may already have taken irreversible actions, may refuse (TaskNotCancelableError), or may finish before the request arrives. Design for 'cancel may not have worked': check the final state, and make side effects idempotent and compensable.
Splitting a system into many communicating agents makes it more modular and robust.

Each network hop between agents adds latency, a failure point, authentication, serialisation of context and another model's reasoning errors. Inside one team and codebase, function calls or in-process sub-agents are almost always cheaper and more reliable. Protocols earn their cost at organisational and trust boundaries.
Another agent's response is trusted data because it came over an authenticated channel.

Authentication tells you who sent it, not that it is safe. A remote agent may itself have read attacker-controlled content, so its messages and artifacts are untrusted input for your model, exactly like a web page or an email.
lab:
Goal: run a toy two-agent exchange over an A2A-style JSON task protocol: discovery through an Agent Card, version checking, idempotent sends keyed by messageId, a task that pauses in input-required, and a follow-up message that completes it. About 10 minutes, Python 3.12 standard library only (it starts a local HTTP server on port 8765).

  1. Save as ag15_lab.py and run it:
import json, threading, time, uuid, urllib.request
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer

CARD = {"name": "Invoice Checker", "version": "1.0.0",
        "supportedInterfaces": [{"url": "http://127.0.0.1:8765/a2a", "protocolBinding": "JSONRPC",
                                 "protocolVersion": "1.0"}],
        "capabilities": {"streaming": False, "pushNotifications": False},
        "skills": [{"id": "check-invoice", "name": "Check an invoice",
                    "description": "Validates totals; asks for the PO number if missing."}]}
TASKS, SEEN = {}, {}                      # task store; messageId -> taskId (idempotency)

def work(task_id, text):
    time.sleep(0.5)                       # pretend to think
    t = TASKS[task_id]
    if t["status"]["state"] == "TASK_STATE_CANCELED":
        return
    if "PO-" not in text:
        t["status"] = {"state": "TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED",
                       "message": {"role": "ROLE_AGENT", "parts": [{"text": "Which PO number?"}]}}
        return
    t["status"] = {"state": "TASK_STATE_COMPLETED"}
    t["artifacts"] = [{"name": "result", "parts": [{"data": {"valid": True, "total": 1180.0}}]}]

class Agent(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def log_message(self, *a): pass
    def reply(self, obj, code=200):
        body = json.dumps(obj).encode(); self.send_response(code)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json"); self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(body)
    def do_GET(self):
        if self.path == "/.well-known/agent-card.json": return self.reply(CARD)
        self.reply({"error": "not found"}, 404)
    def do_POST(self):
        if self.headers.get("A2A-Version", "0.3") != "1.0":
            return self.reply({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": None, "error": {"code": -32009, "message": "VersionNotSupported"}})
        req = json.loads(self.rfile.read(int(self.headers["Content-Length"])))
        p, rid = req.get("params", {}), req["id"]
        if req["method"] == "SendMessage":
            msg = p["message"]
            if msg["messageId"] in SEEN:                       # retry of the same message
                return self.reply({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": rid, "result": {"task": TASKS[SEEN[msg["messageId"]]]}})
            tid = msg.get("taskId") or str(uuid.uuid4())
            TASKS.setdefault(tid, {"id": tid, "contextId": str(uuid.uuid4()), "artifacts": []})
            TASKS[tid]["status"] = {"state": "TASK_STATE_WORKING"}
            SEEN[msg["messageId"]] = tid
            text = " ".join(part.get("text", "") for part in msg["parts"])
            threading.Thread(target=work, args=(tid, text), daemon=True).start()
            return self.reply({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": rid, "result": {"task": TASKS[tid]}})
        if req["method"] == "GetTask":
            return self.reply({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": rid, "result": TASKS[p["id"]]})
        if req["method"] == "CancelTask":
            TASKS[p["id"]]["status"] = {"state": "TASK_STATE_CANCELED"}
            return self.reply({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": rid, "result": TASKS[p["id"]]})
        self.reply({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": rid, "error": {"code": -32601, "message": "Method not found"}})

server = ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 8765), Agent)
threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()

def call(method, params, version="1.0"):
    body = json.dumps({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": str(uuid.uuid4()), "method": method, "params": params}).encode()
    req = urllib.request.Request(CARD["supportedInterfaces"][0]["url"], body,
                                 {"Content-Type": "application/json", "A2A-Version": version})
    return json.loads(urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=5).read())

def wait(task_id, deadline_s=5):
    end = time.time() + deadline_s
    while time.time() < end:
        t = call("GetTask", {"id": task_id})["result"]
        if t["status"]["state"] not in ("TASK_STATE_SUBMITTED", "TASK_STATE_WORKING"):
            return t
        time.sleep(0.1)
    call("CancelTask", {"id": task_id}); raise TimeoutError(task_id)

card = json.loads(urllib.request.urlopen("http://127.0.0.1:8765/.well-known/agent-card.json").read())
print("discovered:", card["name"], [s["id"] for s in card["skills"]])
print("old client:", call("SendMessage", {}, version="0.3").get("error"))

m1 = {"messageId": str(uuid.uuid4()), "role": "ROLE_USER", "parts": [{"text": "Check invoice INV-77, total 1180"}]}
task = call("SendMessage", {"message": m1})["result"]["task"]
retry = call("SendMessage", {"message": m1})["result"]["task"]          # network retry, same messageId
print("same task after retry:", task["id"] == retry["id"])
t = wait(task["id"]); print("state:", t["status"]["state"], "-", t["status"]["message"]["parts"][0]["text"])
m2 = {"messageId": str(uuid.uuid4()), "role": "ROLE_USER", "taskId": task["id"], "parts": [{"text": "PO-5521"}]}
call("SendMessage", {"message": m2})
t = wait(task["id"]); print("state:", t["status"]["state"], "artifact:", t["artifacts"][0]["parts"][0]["data"])
server.shutdown()

What to look for. Discovery prints the agent's name and skill ids from its card. The old client without an A2A-Version: 1.0 header gets error −32009, VersionNotSupported, which is the JSON-RPC code A2A 1.0 assigns to that error (this toy rejects 0.3 rather than supporting it). The retried SendMessage with the same messageId returns the same task id, which is the duplicate protection that prevents double bookings. The first wait ends in input-required with the question "Which PO number?" (a purchase-order number), and the second message, carrying the same taskId, takes the task to completed with a structured artifact. Now break things: send the retry with a new messageId and watch a second task appear; set the worker's sleep to 6 seconds and see the client's deadline cancel the task; and think about what the client should do if the cancel arrives after the work finished.
recap: MCP standardises how one agent uses tools and data it controls; A2A standardises how one agent asks another, opaque agent to do a task; AG-UI standardises how an agent streams to a user interface; AP2 adds payment mandates on top of A2A.
A2A reached its first stable version, 1.0, on 12 March 2026 (1.0.1 on 28 May 2026); it is a Linux Foundation project, and the foundation reported more than 150 supporting organisations in April 2026.

An A2A server publishes an Agent Card, usually at /.well-known/agent-card.json, listing its interfaces and protocol versions, capabilities, security schemes and skills; cards can be signed with JWS over a JCS-canonicalised body.

Work is organised as tasks with eight states: submitted, working, input-required, auth-required, and the terminal completed, failed, canceled and rejected; messages carry parts (text, files, data) and results come back as artifacts.
Eleven operations (send message, send streaming message, get, list, cancel and subscribe to tasks, push-notification config, extended card) are defined once and bound to JSON-RPC, gRPC and HTTP+JSON.
Clients send an A2A-Version header; servers must honour the requested major.minor version, treat an empty header as 0.3, and return VersionNotSupportedError otherwise.
Long tasks are tracked by polling, by streaming (SSE) or by push notifications to a webhook; send-message can return immediately or block until a terminal state.
Cross-vendor trust needs TLS identity, declared security schemes, scoped credentials, in-task authorisation through the auth-required state, and treating remote output as untrusted input.

Design for failure: idempotent sends keyed by messageId, deadlines on your side, cancellation that may not stop work, partial artifacts, and version negotiation errors; and do not split into communicating agents unless a boundary demands it.
glossary: A2A (Agent2Agent)
An open protocol, contributed by Google to the Linux Foundation in 2025, for agents to discover each other and exchange tasks, messages and artifacts.
AG-UI
The Agent-User Interaction Protocol: an event-based protocol for streaming an agent's messages, tool calls and state to a user-facing application.
Agent Card
A JSON document an A2A server publishes describing its name, interfaces, protocol versions, capabilities, security schemes and skills.
AP2
Agent Payments Protocol: an open protocol, used with A2A, in which agents carry cryptographically signed mandates proving a user authorised a purchase.
Artifact
An output produced by an A2A task, such as a document, an image or structured data, made of parts.
Context (A2A)
An identifier that groups related tasks and messages into one conversation.
Extended Agent Card
A more detailed Agent Card returned only to authenticated clients, for skills or details not public.
JCS
JSON Canonicalization Scheme (RFC 8785): a rule for writing JSON in exactly one byte form, so a signature over it can be verified.
JWS
JSON Web Signature (RFC 7515): a standard format for signing JSON content.
Opaque agent
An agent whose internal reasoning, tools and memory are hidden from callers, who see only its declared skills and its outputs.
Part
The smallest unit of content in an A2A message or artifact: text, a file reference or structured data.
Protocol binding
A concrete wire format for the abstract A2A operations: JSON-RPC, gRPC or HTTP+JSON (REST).
Push notification (A2A)
An HTTP POST from the remote agent to a webhook the client registered, carrying task updates for long-running work.
Skill
A capability listed in an Agent Card, with a description, tags, examples and accepted input and output types.
Task (A2A)
The stateful unit of work in A2A, identified by an id and moving through a defined lifecycle of states.
Well-known URI
A standard path on a domain, such as /.well-known/agent-card.json, where clients can find metadata without prior configuration.
drill:
Design: delegating to a supplier's agent

Your procurement agent must ask suppliers' agents to quote and then place orders. Three large suppliers expose A2A 1.0 agents; a dozen small ones only have REST APIs. Orders above $10,000 need a human approver. Design the integration: protocols, discovery, auth, failure handling and security.

Answer

Protocols. For the three A2A suppliers, delegate quoting and ordering as A2A tasks, because their agents negotiate (alternatives, delivery dates, clarifying questions). For the REST-only suppliers, wrap their APIs as MCP tools (or plain API clients); do not invent agents where a deterministic API exists.

Discovery and onboarding. Keep a registry of approved supplier agents: card URL, pinned version, verified JWS signature, allowed skills, data classes you may send. Refresh cards daily and alert on changes; run contract tests against each supplier's sandbox before enabling a new card version.

Auth. Use the security scheme each card declares, with credentials scoped to your organisation and to quoting versus ordering. For orders above $10,000, your side requires human approval before sending the order message; if a supplier's agent moves a task to auth-required (for example to confirm a credit check), route it to the approver, and never treat that state as approval by itself.

Failure handling. Every SendMessage carries a messageId stored with your purchase-order id; retries reuse it. Set deadlines per skill (quotes 10 minutes, orders 1 hour), then cancel and check the final state; reconcile orders against the supplier's order system, because a cancel may arrive after the order was placed. Use push notifications for orders, with authenticated, deduplicated webhook handling. Time out input-required stalls and escalate to a buyer.

Security. Send only what each task needs (no internal budgets or other suppliers' quotes). Validate quote artifacts against a schema; treat any free text from supplier agents as untrusted, never letting it choose your next tool call, and keep supplier output out of contexts that hold other suppliers' data. Log every message and state transition with your trace id for audit.
qa: E
What is the difference between MCP and A2A?

MCP connects an agent to tools and data sources: the calling agent decides what to call, with what arguments, and gets a result back, function by function. A2A connects an agent to another agent: the caller describes a goal, the remote agent decides how to achieve it with its own tools and reasoning, may ask questions, may run for a long time, and returns artifacts. MCP is for capabilities you drive; A2A is for collaborators you delegate to.
E
What is in an A2A Agent Card and where do clients find it?

The agent's name and description, its interfaces (URL, protocol binding such as JSON-RPC, gRPC or HTTP+JSON, and protocol version), provider, capabilities (streaming, push notifications, extended card), security schemes and requirements, default input and output media types, and a list of skills with descriptions, tags and examples. Clients find it at https://{domain}/.well-known/agent-card.json, through registries, or by direct configuration; v1.0 cards can carry JWS signatures.
E
List the A2A task states and which are terminal.

Submitted, working, input-required and auth-required are non-terminal: the task is queued, in progress, waiting for more input from the client, or waiting for authorisation. Completed, failed, canceled and rejected are terminal: no further messages can be sent to the task. Input-required and auth-required are how a remote agent asks its caller for something without ending the task.
M
Walk through a multi-turn A2A exchange on the wire.

The client fetches the Agent Card, picks an interface, and sends SendMessage with a message (role user, parts, a unique messageId) and the A2A-Version header. The agent returns a Task with an id, a contextId and state working. The client polls GetTask, subscribes to a stream, or registers a webhook. The task moves to input-required with an agent message asking, say, for a PO number. The client sends another message with the same taskId. The task moves to working and then completed, with an artifact holding the result.

Follow-up: What if the client's network drops after sending? — Retry SendMessage with the same messageId; the spec lets agents use messageId to detect duplicates, so a well-behaved agent returns the existing task instead of starting a second one.
M
How does authentication and authorisation work between agents from different vendors?

The server's identity comes from TLS on its domain and, optionally, a signed Agent Card. The card declares security schemes (for example OAuth 2.0 or OpenID Connect) and requirements; the client obtains credentials out of band and sends them on each request. The server must authorise every operation and every task access for that client. If work needs further permission mid-task, such as a user's consent to access their data, the task moves to auth-required and the client resolves it; that state change alone authorises nothing. Detailed skills can be kept to an authenticated extended card.
M
What happens when a client and an agent support different A2A versions?

Clients send the A2A-Version header (major.minor, for example 1.0) on every request. The agent must process the request with that version's semantics or return VersionNotSupportedError (JSON-RPC code −32009). An empty header is interpreted as 0.3, so old clients keep working where agents still support 0.3. Agents can expose several interfaces for different versions, which is how migrations proceed.
M
When would you use streaming versus push notifications versus polling for an A2A task?

Streaming (SSE) when the client is online and wants progress in real time, for example to show a user status updates. Push notifications when tasks run for minutes or hours and the client should not hold a connection: the agent POSTs updates to a registered webhook, so the client must be reachable and must verify and deduplicate deliveries. Polling GetTask when neither is available or as a fallback after reconnecting. Blocking SendMessage suits short tasks where the caller simply waits for a terminal state.
M
What do AG-UI and AP2 add to the picture?

AG-UI standardises the last hop to the user: an event-based protocol for an agent to stream messages, tool calls and state changes to a front end, so a UI can render any compliant agent. AP2 addresses payments: it extends A2A so agents can carry signed mandates that prove a user authorised a purchase, giving merchants and payment providers verifiable consent; the Linux Foundation reported more than 60 organisations supporting it in April 2026.
H
Your agent delegates to a vendor's agent over A2A. What are the failure modes and how do you handle them?

Network failures on send: retry with the same messageId so you do not create duplicate tasks. Slow tasks: set your own deadline, then cancel, but treat cancel as best-effort and check the terminal state. Stalls in input-required or auth-required: time out and escalate. Failed or rejected tasks: map to your own error handling and fall back. Partial artifacts: decide whether partial results are usable. Version errors: negotiate or pin. Duplicated push notifications: process idempotently. And semantic failure, where the task completes with a wrong or malicious result: validate artifacts against schemas and treat them as untrusted input.

Follow-up: How do you know where time went across the two systems? — Propagate a correlation id (for example a trace id in message metadata or headers, if both sides agree), and record task ids and state transitions in your own traces.
H
When should you not split a system into multiple communicating agents?

When the agents would live in one team, one codebase and one trust domain. Every protocol hop adds a network round trip, serialisation of context into messages, another model's reasoning errors, authentication, and partial-failure handling, and reliability multiplies down: five hops at 95% each succeed together only 77% of the time. Use function calls, tools or in-process sub-agents instead. Split when there is a real boundary: another organisation, another team that deploys independently, a different trust or compliance domain, or a capability you buy rather than build.
H
How does prompt injection travel across agent boundaries, and what do you do about it?

A remote agent may read attacker-controlled content (a web page, an email, a document) and pass instructions along in its messages or artifacts, intentionally or not. Your agent then reads that text in its context. Treat every message and artifact from another agent as untrusted: never let it directly decide your tool calls, validate structured artifacts against schemas, keep remote content out of contexts that hold private data and an outbound channel, and minimise what you send to remote agents in the first place.
H
Design discovery for a company with 200 internal agents and a dozen external vendor agents.

Use a registry rather than relying on well-known URIs alone: each agent publishes its Agent Card to the registry with owner, environment, version and data-classification metadata; cards are signed and the registry verifies signatures and TLS identity. Clients query the registry by skill and tags, and access is governed by policy (which teams may call which agents, with what scopes). External agents are onboarded through review: contract, security assessment, allowed data classes, and pinned card versions with change alerts. Track usage and errors per agent pair.

t: Agent frameworks compared: what they give you, what they cost, and when to write the loop yourself
sum: What an agent framework actually provides (loop, state, tool schemas, memory, tracing, durability) and costs; graph and state-machine designs versus conversation-driven ones; LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK, Claude Agent SDK, Google ADK, CrewAI and Microsoft Agent Framework as of 9 Oct 2026; the same refund agent sketched in two of them; lock-in; and the 'just write the loop' answer and when it is right.
prereq: ag2
The agent loop calls the model, executes any tool calls it returns, appends the results and repeats until the model answers or a stopping condition (step, token or time budget) fires.
ag3
Tools are described to the model by name, description and JSON Schema; good tools are narrow, return useful errors and make side effects idempotent.
ag7
Control flow can be left to the model or encoded as graphs and state machines with routers, parallel branches and human checkpoints.
ag8
Multi-agent patterns (orchestrator–worker, handoffs, agents as tools) help only when work parallelises or needs isolated context.
ag11
Durable execution checkpoints progress so a run can resume after a crash without repeating side effects.
ag14
Production agents are traced with OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions, so every model and tool call is a span with tokens, latency and errors.
why:
A team starts building an internal agent in early 2025 with the most popular framework of the moment. Six months later they are fighting it: the prompt the model actually receives is assembled somewhere inside the library and they cannot easily see it, a minor upgrade changed how tool errors are reported, and the multi-agent abstraction they adopted because it was there turned a two-tool assistant into four agents passing messages. They rewrite on a second framework. A year after that, the second framework's vendor announces a successor and puts the old one into maintenance mode. The team's actual logic, its tools, prompts and business rules, was never the problem; the scaffolding around it was.

The opposite story is just as common. A team writes its own loop because "it's only thirty lines", then spends a quarter adding checkpointing so long runs survive deploys, a way to pause for human approval and resume the next day, retries that do not double-charge customers, parallel tool calls, streaming to the UI and tracing that shows what happened in step 14 of a failed run. They have built a framework, with fewer users and less testing than the ones they avoided.

Senior interviews ask about this directly: "LangGraph or the OpenAI Agents SDK?", "would you use a framework at all?", "how do you avoid lock-in?". The interviewer is not looking for a favourite library. They want to hear what a framework actually provides, which of those things your system needs, what each choice costs, and how you would stay able to change your mind, because the landscape changes every few months.

This lesson separates what frameworks give you (the loop, state, tool schemas, memory, tracing, durability, human checkpoints, orchestration) from what they cost. It contrasts graph and state-machine designs with conversation-driven ones, surveys the frameworks that matter on 9 October 2026 with their versions verified on that day, sketches the same small refund agent in two of them, works through lock-in, and ends with the "just write the loop yourself" answer and when it is the right one. The lab is that hand-written loop, in the standard library, with a scripted fake model.

One more reason the question matters: the framework decision is often made in the first week of a project, by whoever writes the prototype, and then inherited by everyone who operates the system for years. Making it deliberately, with requirements written down and an exit plan, is one of the cheapest ways a senior engineer can save a team months later.
primer:
Web frameworks, again

Web developers have had this argument for twenty years. You can write a web service directly on the HTTP server interface, use a micro-framework that gives you routing and little else, or use a full framework with an object-relational mapper, authentication, admin pages and migrations. None is right in general. A tiny webhook receiver needs nothing; a large product with many developers benefits from conventions; a high-performance service may outgrow any framework's defaults. Agent frameworks are the same argument, a decade younger and moving much faster. The analogy breaks in one important way: web frameworks are mature, stable and well understood, while agent frameworks are a few years old, change their APIs often, and wrap a component (the model) whose behaviour they cannot fully control. That raises the value of understanding the code underneath.

What sits under any agent

Two ways to own control flow

The deepest difference between frameworks is who decides what happens next. In graph-based designs you draw the flow in code: a node that calls the model, a node that runs tools, a node that checks policy, edges between them, some conditional. The model makes decisions only where the graph lets it. In conversation-driven designs the model decides at every step which tool to call, whether to hand off to another agent, and when it is done; the code supplies tools and guardrails. Graphs are predictable, inspectable and easy to pause at known points; conversations are flexible and short to write. Most real systems mix them, as ag7 describes: a graph for the parts that must happen in order, with free-running agents inside some nodes.

What changes when a model is part of the runtime

Ordinary frameworks orchestrate deterministic code: the same input gives the same path. Agent frameworks orchestrate a component that is non-deterministic, slow, expensive and occasionally wrong. That changes what you want from them. You want to see exactly what the model was given, because most bugs are context bugs. You want to pause and resume, because steps can take minutes and humans may need to approve them. You want to replay and test with a fake model, because real model calls are costly and vary. And you want guardrails in code, because the model cannot be trusted to follow rules on its own. Judge every framework on those four needs before its feature list.

A sixty-second decision

When an interviewer asks "which framework?", a crisp answer runs: "First, do I need durability or human pauses? If yes, a graph framework or our existing workflow engine. If not, is it a single loop with a few tools? Then I write the loop or use a lightweight SDK. If the agent mostly works with files and code on one vendor's model, that vendor's harness is worth a look. In every case, tools, prompts and state stay in our code, and tracing goes to OpenTelemetry, so the choice is reversible." That answer shows you know what frameworks are for and that you plan for change.

A reader who stops here should remember: the loop is small, the hard parts are durability, human checkpoints and observability, and the most important design choice is who owns the control flow.
body:
1. What a framework actually gives you

Strip any agent framework down and you find the loop from ag2: send the conversation and tool schemas to the model; if it returns tool calls, execute them and append the results; repeat until it returns a final answer or a budget runs out. Around that loop, frameworks provide some subset of these, and it pays to know which you need:

CapabilityWhat it isCost to build yourself
LoopCall, run tools, append, repeat, stopTens of lines
Tool schemasJSON Schema generated from function signatures and docstringsSmall; libraries exist
State and memoryConversation history, typed run state, long-term memory hooksSmall to medium
StreamingToken and event streams to a UIMedium (ae10)
TracingSpans per model and tool call with tokens and latencyMedium; OpenTelemetry helps (ag14)
DurabilityCheckpoints after each step; resume after crash or long pauseLarge, unless you have a workflow engine
Human-in-the-loopPause at a step, persist, resume with human inputLarge without durability
OrchestrationHandoffs, sub-agents, parallel branches, graphsMedium to large
Deployment and dev toolsServers, queues, visual debuggers, evaluation hooksLarge

The pattern is clear: the top rows are cheap to build and the bottom rows are expensive. A framework is most valuable when you need the bottom rows, and least valuable when you need only the top.

2. Graph and state-machine designs

In a graph framework, the run has a state (a typed object, often including the message list), and the program is a set of nodes that read and update that state and edges that say which node runs next. A conditional edge picks the next node by inspecting the state, for example "if the last model message contains tool calls, go to the tool node, otherwise end". A checkpointer saves the state after each step, which gives durability and makes interrupts possible: the graph pauses before a node, waits as long as needed for a human, and resumes from the saved state. LangGraph's StateGraph, Microsoft Agent Framework's workflows, Google ADK 2.0's Workflow runtime and CrewAI's Flows all follow this model with different vocabularies.

Graphs shine when the process has required steps (verify identity before changing an address), regulated checkpoints (approval above a threshold), parallel branches with a join, or long waits. They make behaviour inspectable: you can draw the graph and point to where a decision happens. Their cost is rigidity and boilerplate for open-ended tasks, where the "graph" degenerates into "model node, tool node, loop".

3. Conversation-driven designs

In a conversation-driven framework, an agent is a model plus instructions, tools and guardrails, and a runner executes the loop. Multi-agent behaviour comes from handoffs (another agent takes over the conversation) or agents as tools (one agent calls another and gets a result back, keeping control), as described in ag8. The OpenAI Agents SDK, the Claude Agent SDK and CrewAI's Crews work this way. They are concise and flexible: adding a capability means adding a tool or an agent, not redrawing a graph. Their cost is that control flow lives in the model's decisions, so guarantees ("always check the policy before refunding") must be enforced inside tools, guardrails or hooks rather than by the structure of the program.

The picture also explains why teams mix the two. The parts of a process that must happen, in order, with evidence (verify, approve, record) belong in a graph or workflow where they are guaranteed and auditable. The parts that need judgement (understanding a messy request, choosing which records to look at, drafting a reply) belong in a free-running agent inside a node, with its own tools and budget. Asking "which steps must be guaranteed?" before "which framework?" usually decides the architecture, and the framework choice follows from it. A useful test: if a compliance reviewer asked you to prove that a step always happens before another, could you point to code, or only to a prompt? If only to a prompt, that step belongs in the graph.

4. The frameworks that matter, as of 9 October 2026

Versions below are the latest on PyPI on 9 October 2026; check again before relying on any API detail.

  • LangGraph (LangChain; 1.2.14). A graph framework for stateful, long-running agents: StateGraph, nodes and conditional edges, checkpointers for durable execution, interrupts for human-in-the-loop, short- and long-term memory, streaming, and integration with LangSmith for tracing, evaluation and deployment. It can be used without the rest of LangChain.
  • OpenAI Agents SDK (openai-agents 0.23.1). A lightweight, conversation-driven framework whose primitives are agents (instructions, tools, guardrails, handoffs), agents as tools, guardrails for input and output validation, sessions for conversation history, built-in tracing, and newer sandbox agents for working with files and commands. It describes itself as provider-agnostic, supporting OpenAI's Responses and Chat Completions APIs and many other models. Still pre-1.0, so APIs may change.
  • Claude Agent SDK (claude-agent-sdk 0.2.165, Python; a TypeScript version also exists). The harness behind Claude Code as a library: query() for one-shot runs and ClaudeSDKClient for interactive sessions, Claude Code's built-in tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash and others) restricted with an allowed-tools list and permission modes, hooks that run your code before or after tool use, sub-agents, and custom tools defined as Python functions served as in-process MCP servers. Built for Claude models; strongest where agents work with files, code and shells.
  • Google Agent Development Kit (google-adk 2.11.0). ADK 2.0 combines LLM agents with a graph-based Workflow runtime supporting sequential and parallel steps, fan-out and fan-in, loops, retries, state, dynamic nodes, human-in-the-loop and nested workflows, plus a development UI. Optimised for Gemini but model-agnostic, with deployment paths into Google Cloud.
  • CrewAI (1.15.26). Two layers: Crews, teams of role-based agents collaborating with some autonomy, and Flows, event-driven workflows for precise control that can call single LLM steps or whole crews. Popular for role-play-style multi-agent prototypes; Flows add the control production needs.
  • Microsoft Agent Framework (agent-framework 1.21.0; Python and .NET). Agents plus graph-based workflows with sequential, concurrent, handoff and group-collaboration patterns, checkpointing and human-in-the-loop, and a developer UI. Microsoft positions it as the production successor to AutoGen (whose repository is now marked as in maintenance mode) and Semantic Kernel, with migration guides from both.

Others worth knowing: Pydantic AI (2.54.0), type-driven agents from the Pydantic team; AWS's Strands Agents (1.59.0), a model-driven framework; Hugging Face's smolagents (1.26.0), whose agents write Python code as their actions; and LlamaIndex's workflow and agent components for retrieval-heavy systems. Most of these frameworks can consume MCP servers as tools, and several can call or expose A2A agents (ag15); check current docs for specifics.

Claude Agent SDKConversation, sub-agentsClaudeSessions, hooks, permissionsPython, TS
